title: Web3 terms and wallets
summary: A plain-language guide to wallets, identity, tokens and cryptographic proofs.

sections.heading: Wallets and keys
sections.body: A wallet helps manage the credentials used to authorize blockchain transactions. A private key can authorize spending; a public address can be shared to receive assets. Protect recovery credentials and check the destination before sending.

sections.heading: Account abstraction
sections.body: Account abstraction makes it possible to use smart-contract-based account features such as alternative authentication or recovery. ERC-4337 is one approach; available features depend on the wallet.

sections.heading: Identity and tokens
sections.body: Decentralized identifiers (DIDs) are identifiers designed for decentralized identity systems. A soulbound token is a proposed non-transferable token. NFTs represent distinct tokens; fractionalization divides an interest in an NFT into smaller units, subject to the specific arrangement.

sections.heading: Cryptographic proofs
sections.body: Multi-party computation (MPC) lets parties jointly compute a result without each disclosing their private inputs. Zero-knowledge proofs can establish that a statement is valid without revealing all underlying information.

title: Bitcoin
summary: Bitcoin, its network, wallets, mining and halving.

sections.heading: Bitcoin and bitcoin
sections.body: Bitcoin is a peer-to-peer network; bitcoin (BTC) is its native asset. Transactions are signed using private keys and recorded on the blockchain.

sections.heading: Mining and proof of work
sections.body: Miners compete to add blocks using proof of work. Network participants independently verify the rules. Block times vary, and confirmations are not instantaneous.

sections.heading: Wallets and supply
sections.body: A wallet manages the keys needed to authorize transactions rather than holding coins like a physical container. Bitcoin has a maximum supply of 21 million BTC. A satoshi is one hundred-millionth of a bitcoin.

sections.heading: Halving
sections.body: The new bitcoin subsidy for miners is reduced by half at predetermined block intervals. Future calendar dates are estimates because block discovery is variable.

title: Ethereum
summary: Accounts, ether, smart contracts, staking and gas.

sections.heading: Ethereum and ether
sections.body: Ethereum is a blockchain platform for applications and smart contracts. Ether (ETH) is its native asset; tokens can also be issued through contracts on the network.

sections.heading: Accounts and wallets
sections.body: Ethereum accounts can be controlled by keys or by smart-contract code. Wallets provide an interface to accounts and applications; their security and recovery features vary.

sections.heading: Proof of stake and gas
sections.body: Ethereum uses proof of stake, with validators participating in consensus. Transactions consume gas and incur fees; costs and staking returns change over time.

sections.heading: Token standards
sections.body: ERC-20 commonly describes fungible tokens; ERC-721 describes non-fungible tokens; ERC-1155 supports multiple token types in a contract.

title: Stablecoins and digital money
summary: How stablecoins seek to track a reference value and where risks arise.

sections.heading: What is a stablecoin?
sections.body: A stablecoin aims to track a reference value, often a currency. Designs differ: some use reserves, some use crypto collateral, and some rely on algorithmic mechanisms.

sections.heading: Minting and redemption
sections.body: For some reserve-backed stablecoins, authorized participants can create or redeem tokens through an issuer. Individual holders may not have direct redemption rights; check the issuer’s terms.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.body: A peg is not guaranteed. Reserves, custody, liquidity, redemption restrictions, smart-contract flaws and issuer failures can affect value. A central-bank digital currency is different: it is a digital form of sovereign money issued by a central bank.

title: Blockchain layers and rollups
summary: Understand base networks, layer 2 and zero-knowledge rollups.

sections.heading: Layer 1
sections.body: A layer 1 is a base blockchain network with its own rules and consensus mechanism. Bitcoin and Ethereum are examples of distinct base networks.

sections.heading: Layer 2
sections.body: A layer 2 system builds on a base network to process activity differently while relying on the base network for aspects of settlement or security. Specific trust and security assumptions vary by system.

sections.heading: Zero-knowledge rollups
sections.body: A ZK rollup batches transactions outside Ethereum mainnet and submits data and a validity proof to the base layer. This can reduce the amount of computation performed directly on mainnet.

title: Solidity and smart-contract concepts
summary: A reference list of development patterns from the source notes.

sections.heading: Contract architecture
sections.body: Proxy contracts, UUPS, beacon proxies, contract factories and diamond storage are patterns used to structure or upgrade contracts. Their permissions and storage layout need careful review.

sections.heading: Efficiency and data
sections.body: Packed storage, pagination, multicall, large integer arithmetic, Merkle proofs and SSTORE2 are techniques or tools encountered in contract development.

sections.heading: Safety and interaction
sections.body: Checks-effects-interactions, reentrancy guards, pauses, commit-and-reveal schemes and permit-based approvals address different interaction and security concerns. No single pattern guarantees safety.

sections.heading: Further concepts
sections.body: The notes also mention LP tokens, vaults, meta-transactions, deterministic deployment and proofs of inclusion. Consult implementation-specific documentation before using a pattern.

title: Real-world assets and real estate
summary: Explore tokenization and possible uses for property records and transactions.

sections.heading: Real-world assets
sections.body: Tokenization represents an asset or a claim related to an asset using a digital token. What a holder owns depends on the legal documents, custody arrangements and jurisdiction; a token alone does not establish ownership of the underlying asset.

sections.heading: Property applications
sections.body: The source notes explore records, transfers, fractional interests, leases and property management. A blockchain record does not automatically replace a land registry or legal process.

sections.heading: Questions to ask
sections.body: Who owns or holds the asset? What legal rights does the token confer? Who maintains the underlying records? What are the costs, privacy implications and dispute procedures?

title: DAOs and collective governance
summary: A starting point for decentralized autonomous organizations.

sections.heading: What is a DAO?
sections.body: A decentralized autonomous organization coordinates a community around shared rules and decisions, often using smart contracts and proposals. Actual control, participation and legal status vary.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.body: The source notes group organizations around media, social communities, protocols, collecting, services, investment and grants. A DAO can use different mechanisms for membership, voting and treasury management.

sections.heading: Due diligence
sections.body: Review how decisions are made, who controls funds, what code can be upgraded, and any legal or financial obligations. The source document contains historical project names; inclusion would not establish that a project remains active or trustworthy.

title: When might Web3 be useful?
summary: Questions to consider before choosing a blockchain-based approach.

sections.heading: Start with the problem
sections.body: Identify the users, the workflow and the reason independent parties need to coordinate. Consider whether an ordinary database or existing service already solves the problem.

sections.heading: Consider shared records and transfers
sections.body: A blockchain may be relevant when multiple parties need a shared ledger or programmable asset transfer. Compare the benefits against complexity, fees, privacy, governance and recovery requirements.

sections.heading: Test assumptions
sections.body: A smart contract cannot by itself verify off-chain facts, guarantee a legal right or make inaccurate data reliable. Prototype the workflow and examine both technical and legal risks.

title: APIs, HTTP methods and status codes
summary: A practical reference for API styles, HTTP requests, responses and security.

sections.heading: Ways systems communicate
sections.body: REST is an architectural style often used with HTTP. GraphQL lets a client request data using a query language. SOAP uses XML messaging, while gRPC supports remote procedure calls. WebSockets support two-way communication; webhooks notify a receiver when events occur. MQTT and AMQP are messaging protocols.

sections.heading: Common HTTP methods
sections.body: GET retrieves a representation; HEAD requests headers without the response body; POST submits data; PUT creates or replaces a representation; PATCH applies partial changes; DELETE requests removal. OPTIONS describes communication options. CONNECT establishes a tunnel, and TRACE performs a diagnostic loop-back.

sections.heading: Reading status codes
sections.body: 2xx indicates success, 3xx redirection, 4xx a client error, and 5xx a server error. Common examples include 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway and 503 Service Unavailable.

sections.heading: Security basics
sections.body: Use HTTPS, authenticate requests where needed, limit permissions, validate inputs and handle errors safely. Rate limiting and API versioning can help manage reliability and change. Choose authentication and authorization mechanisms appropriate to the system.

title: Load balancing and traffic routing
summary: How servers distribute traffic and why routing strategy matters.

sections.heading: Routing strategies
sections.body: Round robin cycles through available servers. Weighted round robin assigns more traffic to selected servers. Least connections favors servers with fewer active connections; response-time-based strategies use observed latency.

sections.heading: Other approaches
sections.body: Some systems route based on bandwidth or packet measurements. IP hashing can consistently map a client to a server, though changes in the server pool or client addresses can affect that mapping.

sections.heading: Session affinity
sections.body: Sticky sessions route related requests to the same server. They can help applications with local session state, but can make balancing and failover harder. Health checks and capacity limits matter regardless of algorithm.

title: Networking and the OSI model
summary: A layered way to reason about network communication.

sections.heading: The seven layers
sections.body: The OSI model describes physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application layers. Each layer provides a way to reason about a different aspect of communication.

sections.heading: From wire to application
sections.body: Physical and data-link layers handle media and local delivery; the network layer handles routing; the transport layer provides end-to-end communication. Higher layers describe session, representation and application concerns.

sections.heading: Use the model as a guide
sections.body: Real protocols and stacks do not always fit perfectly into a single OSI layer. IP, TCP, UDP, DNS and HTTP address different concerns, and the model is a diagnostic aid rather than a strict deployment diagram.

title: Containers and cloud infrastructure
summary: Images, containers, deployment tools and observability.

sections.heading: Images and containers
sections.body: A container image packages files and configuration used to start a container. A container is an isolated process created from an image. Registries store and distribute images.

sections.heading: Orchestration and infrastructure
sections.body: Orchestration systems manage container workloads. Infrastructure as code describes infrastructure in machine-readable configuration; configuration-management tools help maintain system state.

sections.heading: Observability and delivery
sections.body: Monitoring, logging and related tools help operators understand system behavior. Continuous integration and delivery automate steps in the process of building, checking and releasing software.

sections.heading: Examples in the source notes
sections.body: The notes mention Docker, Kubernetes, Podman, Terraform, Ansible, Grafana, Prometheus, NGINX and GitHub among others. Tool capabilities and offerings change; inclusion is not an endorsement.

title: Types of databases
summary: Compare relational, document, graph, vector and other database models.

sections.heading: Relational and document databases
sections.body: Relational databases organize data into tables and can support SQL queries and transactions. Document databases store records as documents, often with flexible structures. Specific capabilities depend on the product.

sections.heading: Specialized data models
sections.body: Key-value stores retrieve values using keys; graph databases model nodes and relationships; time-series systems are designed for timestamped data; spatial databases support geographic data and queries.

sections.heading: Analytics and search
sections.body: Column-oriented systems can be useful for analytical workloads. Vector databases support similarity searches over vector representations. In-memory systems emphasize fast access, though persistence and durability vary.

sections.heading: Choosing a database
sections.body: Start with data shape, query patterns, consistency, availability, operational effort and cost. A product may support several models; labels alone do not establish its guarantees.

title: SQL: queries, joins and transactions
summary: A compact guide to common SQL operations from the source notes.

sections.heading: Retrieving and filtering
sections.body: SELECT chooses columns; WHERE filters rows; ORDER BY sorts results. Conditions can use comparisons, AND, OR, NOT, BETWEEN, LIKE, IN and EXISTS.

sections.heading: Aggregation and joins
sections.body: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarize values. GROUP BY groups rows, and HAVING filters groups. INNER, LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins combine rows from tables according to a condition.

sections.heading: Window functions
sections.body: Window functions such as ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE, LAG and LEAD operate across related rows using an OVER clause without necessarily collapsing them into one row.

sections.heading: Changing data and structure
sections.body: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE change data. CREATE, ALTER, DROP and TRUNCATE change structures or data; GRANT and REVOKE manage privileges. COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT manage transactions. Exact behavior varies by database.

title: Vector databases and retrieval
summary: The journey from source data to similarity search results.

sections.heading: Prepare and embed
sections.body: Collect source material such as text, code or images. Larger documents may be split into chunks, then an embedding model converts each item into a vector. Metadata can retain source and access information.

sections.heading: Index and search
sections.body: Store vectors in an index suited to a distance or similarity measure. Convert a query using a compatible embedding model, then retrieve candidates; approximate nearest-neighbor methods can trade some accuracy for speed.

sections.heading: Rank and use results
sections.body: Filter and optionally rerank candidates, then return the most relevant items with their sources to the application. Test retrieval quality, access controls, freshness and latency for the actual workload.

title: Software development and testing
summary: A guide to delivery practices and common kinds of tests.

sections.heading: Development and delivery
sections.body: A software lifecycle typically includes understanding requirements, design, implementation, testing, release and maintenance. Agile and DevOps describe practices for iterative delivery and collaboration; teams adapt them to their needs.

sections.heading: Functional and integration tests
sections.body: Smoke tests check whether basic functionality works. Functional tests compare behavior against requirements; integration tests check how components work together. Regression tests help detect unintended changes to existing behavior.

sections.heading: Performance and security tests
sections.body: Load tests examine behavior under expected demand; stress tests explore behavior beyond normal capacity. Security testing investigates relevant threats, while fuzz testing supplies unexpected or malformed inputs to discover failures.

sections.heading: User-interface tests
sections.body: UI tests exercise user interactions and can check important accessibility or responsive behavior. Select tests according to risk and the kind of change rather than treating any one test type as complete coverage.

title: Cybersecurity: threats, defenses and assessment
summary: Explore common threats, protective controls and questions for assessing an organization.

sections.heading: Start with threats
sections.body: Learn how phishing, ransomware, denial of service and application attacks work, then explore interception and spoofing. Each attack can have multiple paths; diagrams are simplified examples.

sections.heading: Build layers of protection
sections.body: Use access controls, secure development, network protection, monitoring and tested recovery plans together. Choose safeguards based on the systems and risks involved.

sections.heading: Assess and improve
sections.body: Use the security questionnaire to identify questions, owners, evidence and follow-up actions. An answer alone does not establish that a control is effective or that an organization is certified.

title: Common cyberattacks
summary: Recognize common attack patterns and ways to reduce exposure.

sections.heading: Phishing
sections.body: Deceptive messages or websites attempt to make people disclose information or take harmful actions. Example: deceptive message → fake sign-in page → stolen credentials → account misuse. Verify requests through a known channel and use phishing-resistant authentication where feasible.

sections.heading: Ransomware
sections.body: Ransomware can encrypt files or disrupt systems and demand payment; attackers may also steal data. Example: malicious attachment → compromised device → data encrypted → ransom demand. Restrict access, update systems and test isolated backups and recovery.

sections.heading: Denial of service
sections.body: A denial-of-service attack exhausts resources or disrupts service; a distributed attack uses multiple sources. Capacity planning, rate limits, filtering and upstream mitigation can reduce impact, but do not guarantee availability.

sections.heading: SQL injection and cross-site scripting
sections.body: SQL injection occurs when untrusted input changes a database query’s meaning. Parameterized queries and least privilege help prevent it. Cross-site scripting occurs when untrusted content executes as code in a user’s browser; context-appropriate output encoding and safe frameworks help reduce risk.

sections.heading: Zero-day exploits
sections.body: A zero-day exploit targets a vulnerability before a fix is available or before defenders have had an opportunity to apply it. Monitor advisories, limit exposure and apply available mitigations; the timeline differs by incident.

title: Network interception and spoofing
summary: Understand impersonation, traffic interception and practical safeguards.

sections.heading: Interception and sniffing
sections.body: A person positioned on a network path may observe or alter traffic. Packet capture can be legitimate administration or malicious surveillance; unencrypted content is particularly exposed. Use authenticated encryption such as HTTPS and verify certificate warnings.

sections.heading: DNS spoofing
sections.body: A forged DNS response or compromised resolver can direct a request to an unintended address. Example: user requests a domain → false DNS answer → connection to an attacker-controlled destination. HTTPS certificate validation and trustworthy DNS infrastructure provide complementary protection.

sections.heading: ARP spoofing
sections.body: On a local network an attacker may send false ARP messages associating the attacker’s hardware address with another device’s IP address. This can redirect traffic. Network segmentation and switch protections can help; encrypted connections still matter.

sections.heading: Spoofing more broadly
sections.body: Spoofing means impersonating an identity or source, such as an email sender, address or device. The right defense depends on the protocol and trust boundary.

title: Security controls and operations
summary: A practical overview of controls across people, systems and recovery.

sections.heading: Governance and access
sections.body: Assign owners, inventory assets and assess risk. Grant the access needed for a role, review it regularly and use strong authentication. Keep policies and awareness training relevant to actual operations.

sections.heading: Networks, cloud and devices
sections.body: Firewalls filter traffic using rules such as address, port, protocol or connection state; application-aware controls can inspect higher-level traffic. An intrusion prevention system detects and can block suspicious activity. Segment networks and manage endpoint and cloud configurations.

sections.heading: Applications and data
sections.body: Protect sensitive data in transit and at rest, manage secrets, validate inputs, review dependencies and test application changes. Retention and privacy requirements depend on the data and context.

sections.heading: Monitoring and recovery
sections.body: Collect and protect useful logs, investigate alerts and plan incident response. Test backups and restoration, assign responsibilities and coordinate with service providers. Periodic exercises expose gaps before an incident.

sections.heading: Review suppliers and physical access
sections.body: Assess suppliers according to the data and systems they handle. Consider physical access, staff onboarding and offboarding, vulnerability management and updates alongside technical controls.

summary: Search questions across 13 areas to guide an evidence-based security review.

sections.heading: How to use this questionnaire
sections.body: Search the questions below, identify a responsible owner and request evidence such as policies, configuration records, audit findings or test results. Record gaps and follow-up actions in your own approved system.

sections.heading: Interpret answers carefully
sections.body: Questions are adapted from a supplied questionnaire. Its organization-specific answers are not included. The questions are prompts, not a certification, compliance determination or complete assessment; adapt them to your organization and obligations.

title: Science and quantum: a starting point
summary: Explore quantum information, cryptography, light, time, gravity and the expanding universe.

sections.heading: Two paths to explore
sections.body: Quantum technology explores how quantum physics can be used for computation and communication. Physics and the universe looks at light, extremely short times, gravity and cosmic expansion.

sections.heading: Connecting the ideas
sections.body: Entanglement is a quantum relationship; quantum key distribution uses quantum states to help establish keys. Post-quantum cryptography uses mathematical algorithms designed for ordinary computers and resistant to attacks involving quantum computers.

sections.heading: What remains uncertain
sections.body: Experiments support quantum mechanics and general relativity across many conditions, but researchers continue to investigate how gravity and quantum physics fit together and why cosmic expansion is accelerating.

title: Quantum entanglement and key distribution
summary: How entangled systems are related and how quantum states can help establish shared keys.

sections.heading: Entanglement
sections.body: Entangled systems are described by a joint quantum state: measurements can show correlations stronger than classical explanations of a particular kind allow. Outcomes are individually unpredictable, and entanglement cannot be used on its own to send a controllable message faster than light.

sections.heading: Quantum key distribution
sections.body: Quantum key distribution (QKD) uses quantum states, often carried by photons, and a classical communication channel to help two parties establish a shared secret key. Some protocols use entanglement; others do not. The key can then be used with conventional encryption.

sections.heading: A simplified flow
sections.body: Prepare or share quantum states → measure and compare selected information over an authenticated classical channel → estimate errors → derive a key if the checks succeed. An eavesdropper can disturb states, but noise also causes errors.

sections.heading: Limits in practice
sections.body: Security depends on the protocol, authenticated classical communication, devices and implementation assumptions. QKD is a method for key distribution, not a complete security system; range, cost and hardware constraints matter.

title: Shor’s algorithm and quantum computing
summary: Why a quantum factoring algorithm matters for public-key cryptography.

sections.heading: The idea
sections.body: Shor’s algorithm uses a quantum computer to find the period of a suitable mathematical function; classical steps use that information to help factor an integer. Related quantum techniques can solve discrete logarithms efficiently.

sections.heading: Why security teams care
sections.body: A sufficiently capable, error-corrected quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could undermine RSA and widely used elliptic-curve public-key schemes. It does not mean all encryption breaks or that today’s machines can break deployed keys at scale.

sections.heading: Prepare for a transition
sections.body: Identify systems that depend on vulnerable public-key algorithms and data that must remain confidential for many years. Plan and test migration with maintained implementations and current standards. The timing of a sufficiently capable machine is uncertain.

title: Lattices, ML-KEM and SLH-DSA
summary: A guide to lattice mathematics and two post-quantum cryptography standards.

sections.heading: Lattices and multiplication
sections.body: A lattice is a regular mathematical arrangement of points generated by combining basis vectors with integer coefficients. Matrix and polynomial multiplication are useful building blocks in structured lattice schemes. Their security does not come from multiplication alone: ML-KEM relies on the difficulty of the module learning with errors problem.

sections.heading: ML-KEM: establish a shared key
sections.body: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM), standardized in NIST FIPS 203, lets parties establish shared secret key material over a public channel. A symmetric algorithm can then use derived key material to protect data. A KEM by itself does not authenticate the parties.

sections.heading: SLH-DSA: verify signatures
sections.body: Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (SLH-DSA), standardized in NIST FIPS 205, signs messages so recipients can verify authenticity and integrity. It uses hash-based constructions; stateless means the signer need not maintain a changing state between signatures. It is not a key-encapsulation mechanism.

sections.heading: Security and implementation
sections.body: These algorithms are designed to resist known attacks from both classical and quantum computers; no algorithm offers an unconditional guarantee against future discoveries or implementation errors. Use established libraries, suitable parameters and current guidance.

title: The speed of light and attoseconds
summary: Explore a fundamental speed and a remarkably short unit of time.

sections.heading: The speed of light
sections.body: In a vacuum light travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second, denoted c. Light travels more slowly through materials; the local speed limit for transmitting information in relativity remains c in vacuum.

sections.heading: An attosecond
sections.body: One attosecond is 10⁻¹⁸ seconds: one billionth of a billionth of a second. In a vacuum, light travels about 0.3 nanometres in an attosecond—on the scale of atoms.

sections.heading: Why measure such brief intervals?
sections.body: Ultrashort light pulses allow scientists to study electron dynamics in matter. The pulses help resolve very fast changes; their existence does not mean that information moves faster than light.

title: Gravity and the expanding universe
summary: How gravity shapes spacetime and why distant galaxies can recede faster than light.

sections.heading: Gravity and spacetime
sections.body: Newton’s gravity describes many everyday and astronomical situations well. General relativity describes gravity through the geometry of spacetime, shaped by matter and energy; it successfully predicts effects including gravitational lensing and gravitational waves.

sections.heading: Expanding space
sections.body: On large scales, the universe expands: distances between sufficiently distant, roughly comoving galaxies grow as space expands. Bound systems such as galaxies are not simply stretched in the same way.

sections.heading: Faster than light?
sections.body: For sufficiently distant galaxies, the rate at which their distance increases due to cosmic expansion can exceed the speed of light. This does not mean a nearby object or a signal travels locally through space faster than light; recession speed depends on how cosmological distance is defined.

sections.heading: Open questions
sections.body: Observations indicate accelerating expansion, often modeled using dark energy. Its nature remains uncertain, and different methods of estimating today’s expansion rate give values that are in tension.

title: Payments: a starting point
summary: Understand the payment journey, the companies involved and how to compare providers.

sections.heading: Start with the transaction
sections.body: Follow a card payment from checkout through authorization, clearing and settlement. Actual flows vary by payment method, market and provider.

sections.heading: Understand the stack
sections.body: Gateways, processors, acquirers and other services can be supplied by separate companies or combined in a single platform. Roles and responsibilities depend on the contract and market.

sections.heading: Compare providers
sections.body: Explore the directory as a starting point. Check whether a provider supports your country, business type, payment methods, currencies and integration before relying on it.

title: How a card payment works
summary: Follow a simplified card transaction from checkout to payout.

sections.heading: Checkout and authorization
sections.body: A customer presents a card at checkout. The merchant’s payment services send an authorization request through the relevant payment participants and network to the issuer. The issuer approves or declines; approval is not the same as final settlement.

sections.heading: Capture and clearing
sections.body: The merchant or its provider submits eligible transaction details for capture and clearing. The payment network and participants exchange the information needed to calculate obligations. Timing and the exact sequence vary.

sections.heading: Settlement and payout
sections.body: Settlement moves funds between participating financial institutions. The merchant’s provider then pays the merchant under its terms, potentially after fees, reserves or adjustments. Payout timing varies.

sections.heading: Disputes and refunds
sections.body: A refund is generally initiated by the merchant. A cardholder may instead dispute a transaction with the issuer, potentially starting a chargeback process. Rules, evidence requirements and deadlines depend on the network and circumstances.

title: The payment stack: roles and services
summary: Compare gateways, processors, facilitators, orchestration and supporting services.

sections.heading: Checkout, gateways and terminals
sections.body: An independent software vendor (ISV) builds software that can integrate payments. A gateway securely transmits transaction data between checkout and payment services. Terminal management helps deploy, update and monitor payment devices.

sections.heading: Processors, acquirers and networks
sections.body: A processor handles payment transaction processing. An acquirer enables merchants to accept card transactions and participates in clearing and settlement; card networks connect participants under their rules. Routing and switching direct transaction messages to appropriate destinations.

sections.heading: PSPs and payment facilitators
sections.body: A payment service provider (PSP) offers merchants payment services, often combining multiple functions. A payment facilitator (PayFac) typically onboards and manages sub-merchants under an acquiring relationship. Exact responsibilities and legal arrangements differ.

sections.heading: Orchestration and supporting services
sections.body: An orchestration layer coordinates connections and routing across payment providers. Fraud tools help assess risk; dispute services help manage chargebacks; billing and analytics software supports subscription and reporting workflows. One provider may offer several of these functions.

sections.heading: Questions to ask
sections.body: Confirm the contracting entity, supported locations, onboarding and underwriting, payment methods, fees, settlement currency and timing, data portability, security responsibilities, dispute handling and support. A listed brand is not a recommendation.

title: Payment provider directory

title: Linux: remote access and development
summary: Use SSH, Git, Python environments and persistent terminal sessions.

sections.heading: SSH and credentials
sections.body: Generate an SSH key and protect the private key. Add only the public key to the intended account. Verify host identity when connecting, and use port forwarding only when needed.

sections.heading: Git and Python
sections.body: Use SSH or a credential manager for Git; avoid tokens in URLs or shell history. Git’s store helper saves credentials in plaintext. Install Python dependencies inside a virtual environment rather than overriding system packages.

sections.heading: Long-running work
sections.body: A terminal multiplexer can preserve sessions when a connection drops. nohup can keep a process running after logout, but is not a full service manager. For production services, use an appropriate supervisor and logging policy.

sections.heading: Local models
sections.body: Ollama commands can list and run locally available models; model behavior, hardware needs and command options vary by version.

title: Linux maintenance and cleanup
summary: A cautious approach to updates, networking, storage and containers.

sections.heading: Updates and recovery
sections.body: Package and release upgrades depend on the distribution. Review the proposed changes, verify backups and plan recovery before upgrading. Do not remove core packages or disable logging, time synchronization and automatic updates as a generic cleanup recipe.

sections.heading: Network changes
sections.body: A mistaken network change can cut off remote access. On systems using Netplan, netplan try can roll back unconfirmed changes; verify the rollback and keep an independent recovery path.

sections.heading: Docker cleanup
sections.body: Inspect disk use and containers before deleting anything. Pruning can remove stopped containers, images or persistent volumes; unused does not necessarily mean unneeded. Back up data and target a specific resource.

sections.heading: Memory, swap and logs
sections.body: Linux uses spare memory for cache and generally manages it automatically. Do not routinely clear caches, remove swap or erase logs to make free-memory numbers look larger. Review retention and capacity needs before changes.

title: Privacy and security operating systems
summary: Compare approaches to security, compartmentalization and online privacy.

sections.heading: Different purposes
sections.body: Debian and Fedora are general-purpose systems with security features, not anonymity systems by default. Qubes OS isolates activities in separate compartments and requires compatible hardware. Tails is a portable live system designed for privacy and routes connections through Tor.

sections.heading: Isolation and security
sections.body: Whonix uses a gateway and workstation architecture with Tor, typically in virtual machines. Kicksecure focuses on hardening. Parrot includes security and privacy-oriented tools; its editions serve different purposes.

sections.heading: Check current details
sections.body: The original notes also list MOFO Linux and Kodachi. Their current maintenance, official download location and security properties need independent verification. For every option, check recent updates, hardware requirements, documentation, threat model and authentic downloads.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.body: No operating system guarantees anonymity or safety. Identity disclosure, browser behavior, compromised hardware and configuration can still matter.

title: Virtual worlds and the metaverse: a timeline
summary: Explore selected milestones in virtual worlds, immersive technology and digital ownership.

sections.heading: What is the metaverse?
sections.body: The term is used for different visions of shared digital spaces, often involving persistent worlds, social interaction and user-created content. Virtual reality, games and blockchains can be involved, but none is required in every definition.

sections.heading: 1992–2003: fiction and virtual communities
sections.body: Neal Stephenson’s 1992 novel Snow Crash popularized the term metaverse. Linden Lab released the shared virtual world Second Life in 2003; it allowed people to socialize and build within a digital environment.

sections.heading: 2006–2015: platforms and digital infrastructure
sections.body: Roblox’s history of user-created experiences extends to 2006. Ethereum launched in 2015, providing a programmable blockchain used by some applications for digital assets. A shared virtual world does not inherently require a blockchain.

sections.heading: 2021 onward: renewed attention
sections.body: In 2021 the Facebook company adopted the name Meta and described its vision for the metaverse. Virtual worlds and immersive tools continue to evolve, and interoperability, privacy, governance and access remain open questions.

title: AI, made easier to explore
summary: Follow a clear path from the basics to working models, practical systems and responsible use.

sections.heading: A useful place to begin
sections.body: Artificial intelligence brings together data, mathematics and software to solve problems. Start with the foundations, then follow the topics that match what you want to understand or build.

sections.heading: Learn by following the connections
sections.body: A prediction begins with data, passes through a model and is evaluated against an objective. Generative AI systems can add retrieval and tools; their performance and risks depend on the whole system.

title: What is AI? A guide to the basics
summary: Understand the relationship between AI, machine learning and deep learning, and when each is useful.

sections.heading: AI, machine learning and deep learning
sections.body: Artificial intelligence covers computational methods for tasks associated with perception, reasoning, language or decision-making. Machine learning learns patterns from data; deep learning uses multilayer neural networks. These categories overlap rather than forming a strict test of intelligence.

sections.heading: Learning approaches
sections.body: Supervised learning uses examples with target labels; unsupervised learning looks for structure without those labels. Reinforcement learning studies decisions and feedback from an environment. Transfer learning adapts previously learned representations to another task.

sections.heading: Common tasks and models
sections.body: Classification predicts categories, regression predicts numerical values, clustering groups similar cases, and dimensionality reduction represents data in fewer dimensions. Trees, random forests, linear models, nearest neighbors and neural networks have different assumptions and trade-offs.

sections.heading: A practical roadmap
sections.body: Learn basic Python, linear algebra, probability and data handling; build a baseline, evaluate on held-out data, then study neural networks and deployment. Choose topics based on the problem instead of assuming a larger model is always better.

title: From data to a working model
summary: Follow the decisions that turn raw data into a useful, maintainable machine-learning system.

sections.heading: Frame and prepare
sections.body: Define the decision, users, success measure and constraints. Inventory data sources and permissions, understand collection and missingness, clean and label data where appropriate, and keep records of transformations.

sections.heading: Split and evaluate
sections.body: Separate training, validation and test data in a way that reflects deployment; group or time-based splits can be important. Avoid leakage across splits. Compare against simple baselines and inspect performance for relevant groups and failure cases.

sections.heading: Production and feedback
sections.body: Version data, models and code; deploy with appropriate access controls; monitor quality, cost, latency and drift. A change in inputs does not automatically mean model performance has degraded: measure both and investigate.

sections.heading: People and context
sections.body: Data engineers, analysts, scientists, ML engineers and domain experts contribute different skills. Role boundaries vary, and a practical project needs both technical and operational ownership.

title: Inside a neural network: a worked example
summary: Follow one calculation from inputs and weights to an output, then count the parameters in a small network.

sections.heading: One neuron
sections.body: Given x = [2, 1, 3], weights w = [1, −1, 1] and bias b = −5, the weighted sum is 2 − 1 + 3 − 5 = −1. ReLU(z) = max(0, z), so the output is 0. This is a simple illustrative neuron, not a trained model.

sections.heading: Layers and dimensions
sections.body: A dense layer with 3 inputs and 4 outputs uses a 4 × 3 weight matrix and 4 biases: 16 parameters. A following dense layer with 4 inputs and 2 outputs adds 8 weights and 2 biases: 10 more, or 26 total. Counts assume each layer includes biases.

sections.heading: Forward and backward passes
sections.body: A forward pass computes predictions and a loss. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to calculate gradients; an optimizer uses those gradients and its update rule to adjust parameters. A zero gradient alone does not prove a global optimum.

sections.heading: Other activations and training choices
sections.body: Sigmoid maps real numbers to values between 0 and 1; softmax produces a distribution across a set of scores. Dropout and regularization can help generalization, but effects depend on the setting. Batch normalization normally includes numerical stability and learned per-feature scale and shift.

title: A field guide to neural network architectures
summary: Compare the structures used for sequences, images, graphs, generation and more.

sections.heading: Dense and recurrent networks
sections.body: A multilayer perceptron applies learned transformations and nonlinearities. Recurrent networks update a state across a sequence; LSTMs use gates to manage information. State-space models are another sequence-model family with their own design choices.

sections.heading: Images, graphs and residual connections
sections.body: Convolutional networks use local filters to process grid-like data; graph neural networks combine information from neighboring nodes. Residual connections add a path around a transformation, helping information and gradients flow in deep networks.

sections.heading: Generative approaches
sections.body: Autoencoders learn representations that can reconstruct input. GANs train a generator and discriminator in competition. Diffusion models learn a denoising process; different systems make different architectural and training choices.

sections.heading: Mixture of experts
sections.body: A router chooses which expert components process an input or token. Routing and capacity choices influence compute and behavior; examples in the notes are simplified and should not be read as a specification for every model.

title: How transformers and language models work
summary: Explore tokens, attention and generation without losing sight of what a model can and cannot tell you.

sections.heading: Tokens and embeddings
sections.body: A tokenizer maps text to token IDs; tokens need not correspond one-to-one with words. An embedding maps tokens or other inputs into vectors. Model architecture and training determine what those representations capture.

sections.heading: Self-attention
sections.body: A transformer computes query, key and value representations. Attention scores compare queries and keys, are scaled and normalized, and weight values to combine information. Masks and context limits determine which positions can interact.

sections.heading: Generating language
sections.body: Many language models predict a distribution over a next token given context. A decoding method selects a token and repeats. Sampling, temperature and other settings can change output; fluent text is not proof of accuracy.

sections.heading: Adapting and multimodal learning
sections.body: Fine-tuning changes parameters with additional training; prompting changes the input without necessarily changing model weights. Multimodal systems can process combinations such as text and images; encoder and model details vary.

title: RAG, vector search and AI agents
summary: See how language models use external information and tools—and where those systems can fail.

sections.heading: Retrieval-augmented generation
sections.body: A retrieval system finds potentially relevant information and supplies it to a model as context. Embeddings and vector search are one possible retrieval method; keyword and hybrid approaches are also useful. Good retrieval does not guarantee factual output.

sections.heading: From documents to answers
sections.body: Prepare and chunk documents, retain metadata and access controls, index content, retrieve and optionally rerank candidates, then evaluate whether answers are supported by the retrieved material. Handle stale, incomplete or malicious content.

sections.heading: Agents and tools
sections.body: An agentic system can choose or sequence actions using tools and feedback. Bound tool permissions, validate inputs and outputs, cap resource use, protect credentials, and require appropriate human approval for consequential actions.

sections.heading: Safety and evaluation
sections.body: Treat external text as untrusted, including retrieved passages. Test prompt injection and permission boundaries; log only what is necessary under a privacy policy. Evaluate end-to-end outcomes and tool use rather than only model responses.

title: Probability and statistics for AI
summary: A practical introduction to uncertainty, distributions, inference and model measurement.

sections.heading: Describe and visualize data
sections.body: Means, medians, spread, histograms and plots summarize data in different ways. Inspect distributions and outliers; datasets with similar summary statistics can still look very different.

sections.heading: Probability and inference
sections.body: Bernoulli and binomial models describe certain binary outcomes, normal distributions describe many continuous approximations, and Poisson models can describe event counts under specified assumptions. A p-value concerns results at least as extreme under a null model; it is not the probability the null is true.

sections.heading: Evaluate predictions
sections.body: Classification accuracy, precision and recall answer different questions; confusion matrices show error types. Regression metrics include mean absolute error and root-mean-square error. Compare metrics with the costs of different mistakes.

sections.heading: Optimization and search
sections.body: Gradient descent updates parameters using a loss gradient. Evolutionary algorithms, simulated annealing and particle swarms are broader search methods with distinct assumptions. A method’s usefulness depends on the objective, constraints and compute budget.

title: AI risk and governance
summary: Identify failures, assign ownership and design safeguards around the people affected.

sections.heading: Map risks to use
sections.body: Consider inaccurate outputs, biased outcomes, privacy exposure, data quality, model drift, availability, cost and downstream consequences. The importance of each risk depends on the application, people affected and deployment context.

sections.heading: Protect agentic systems
sections.body: Prompt injection, excessive permissions, insecure tools and uncontrolled loops can turn an incorrect answer into an action. Separate instructions from untrusted data where possible, enforce permissions outside the model, set limits and audit consequential actions.

sections.heading: Govern and respond
sections.body: Assign accountable owners; document intended use and limitations; evaluate before and after deployment; define incident response, rollback and human oversight. NIST’s AI RMF organizes activities as Govern, Map, Measure and Manage.

sections.heading: Regulatory claims
sections.body: The EU AI Act has different requirements, exceptions and dates for different systems and roles. The original notes contain outdated or overgeneralized claims. Consult the current legislation and qualified advice for a specific use; this guide is not a compliance determination.

title: Neural networks by example
summary: Work through a neuron, a small network and the training loop, step by step.

sections.heading: Start with a single neuron
sections.body: Take three inputs: 2, 1 and 3. Multiply them by weights 1, −1 and 1; then add a bias of −5. The result is −1. Applying ReLU, which replaces negative values with zero, gives an output of 0.

sections.heading: Add another layer
sections.body: A dense layer with three inputs and four outputs has 12 weights and four biases: 16 parameters. A second layer with four inputs and two outputs adds eight weights and two biases. The complete two-layer network has 26 parameters.

sections.heading: Follow the training loop
sections.body: Compute a prediction in a forward pass, compare it with the target using a loss function, then use backpropagation to calculate how changes in the parameters affect that loss. An optimizer uses those gradients to update the parameters.

sections.heading: Where the simplification ends
sections.body: The example uses a tiny fully connected network and assumes both layers have biases. Real architectures can share weights, use different activations or omit biases. A gradient of zero does not by itself prove that a global optimum has been found.

title: AI concepts: a practical glossary
summary: Find clear definitions and pathways to deeper guides across machine learning, generative AI and statistics.

sections.heading: How to use this glossary
sections.body: Browse the ideas by topic, then follow the links to explanations and worked examples. Related terms are grouped by meaning so that you can find the concept you need without working through a long list.

sections.heading: Definitions in context
sections.body: Definitions are starting points. Algorithms, model architectures and evaluation methods have assumptions that change how they should be applied.

title: How machines learn: methods compared
summary: Choose between supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning by the problem and feedback available.

sections.heading: Supervised learning
sections.body: A model learns from examples with known targets. Classification predicts a category; regression predicts a number. Labels need not be perfect, so review their quality and how they were obtained.

sections.heading: Unsupervised learning
sections.body: Clustering looks for structure without target labels; dimensionality reduction represents data using fewer dimensions. A cluster is a mathematical grouping, not automatically a meaningful real-world category.

sections.heading: Reinforcement learning
sections.body: An agent takes actions in an environment and receives feedback in the form of rewards. The goal is to learn a policy over time; a reward is a designed signal and can miss the outcome people actually value.

sections.heading: Transfer and pretraining
sections.body: A model can learn general representations on one dataset and be adapted to another task. Fine-tuning changes model parameters; using examples in a prompt does not necessarily retrain the model.

title: How to evaluate a machine-learning model
summary: Choose measures that match the mistakes your application can afford.

sections.heading: Start with a fair comparison
sections.body: Set aside representative evaluation data, define a simple baseline and decide what success means before tuning. Prevent the same person, future event or duplicated record from leaking across splits.

sections.heading: Classification
sections.body: Accuracy counts all correct predictions. Precision asks how many predicted positives were correct; recall asks how many actual positives were found. A confusion matrix separates false positives and false negatives, which can have very different consequences.

sections.heading: Regression and uncertainty
sections.body: Mean absolute error averages the size of errors; root mean squared error gives larger errors more weight. Examine error distributions and subgroups as well as a single score. A model’s reported confidence can itself require calibration.

sections.heading: Generalization and drift
sections.body: Overfitting occurs when a model fits training data but performs worse on new data; underfitting misses useful patterns. Monitor both input changes and actual outcomes—data drift alone does not prove performance has degraded.

sections.heading: Read the whole evaluation workflow
sections.body: The supplied process diagram suggests a 70/30 split, but that is an example rather than a universal rule. Fit feature selection and hyperparameter searches inside the training/validation process, then preserve a final test set. Matthews correlation coefficient combines all four binary confusion-matrix counts: (TP×TN−FP×FN)/√((TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)), with an explicit convention required for a zero denominator.

title: From prompt to answer: language models and retrieval
summary: Trace the journey from input tokens through retrieval, generation and verification.

sections.heading: Prompt and tokens
sections.body: A tokenizer turns input into token IDs, which a model represents as vectors. Tokens are not always whole words. Context length limits what can be considered in a particular request.

sections.heading: Predict and generate
sections.body: Many language models predict a distribution for the next token. A decoding method chooses a token, adds it to the context and repeats. A plausible answer can still contain fabricated or unsupported details.

sections.heading: Bring in external information
sections.body: Retrieval-augmented generation finds potentially relevant material and supplies it to the model. Chunking, access permissions, retrieval quality, freshness and citations matter. Retrieval improves access to information but cannot guarantee correctness.

sections.heading: Check the result
sections.body: Test whether retrieved evidence supports the answer, including cases with no relevant source. Treat retrieved documents and tool outputs as untrusted input, and enforce data permissions outside the model.

title: Computer vision and multimodal AI
summary: Explore how systems work with images, text and other forms of data.

sections.heading: From pixels to features
sections.body: Images can be represented as arrays of pixel values. Computer vision methods use features to support tasks such as classification, object detection and segmentation. Performance depends on the dataset and conditions of use.

sections.heading: Learning shared representations
sections.body: A multimodal model can encode text and images into representations that are compared or combined. Contrastive training can bring matching examples closer in a learned space; similarity is not proof that an image or caption is true.

sections.heading: Beyond a single image
sections.body: Some systems use video frames, audio or sensor data alongside text. Their architectures vary; a language model with an image input is not necessarily able to perceive the world like a person.

sections.heading: Practical limits
sections.body: Evaluate lighting, image quality, accessibility, privacy and performance across relevant populations. A model trained on one setting can fail in another.

title: How generative models create content
summary: Compare autoregressive models, autoencoders, GANs and diffusion.

sections.heading: Autoregressive generation
sections.body: A model predicts one element conditioned on earlier elements. Language models commonly generate tokens this way; the choices made at each step shape the rest of the sequence.

sections.heading: Autoencoders
sections.body: An encoder produces a representation from an input and a decoder attempts to reconstruct it. A bottleneck can encourage a compact representation, but reconstruction alone does not guarantee useful or interpretable features.

sections.heading: GANs
sections.body: A generator produces samples while a discriminator learns to distinguish real and generated examples. Training balances two objectives; the discriminator’s score should not automatically be treated as a calibrated probability.

sections.heading: Diffusion
sections.body: A diffusion model learns to reverse a noise process and can generate a sample through iterative denoising. The steps, conditioning and representation depend on the system. Simplified diagrams do not establish the internals of a proprietary product.

title: Statistical inference and uncertainty
summary: Understand sampling, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests and common interpretation errors.

sections.heading: Samples and populations
sections.body: A sample provides incomplete information about a population. Random sampling, stratification and a clear definition of the population can help; neither a large sample nor a complex model automatically removes bias.

sections.heading: Confidence intervals
sections.body: A confidence interval is produced by a procedure designed to cover a fixed population parameter at a specified long-run rate under its assumptions. Its width depends on the data, method and confidence level.

sections.heading: Hypothesis tests
sections.body: A p-value is the probability, assuming the null model and its assumptions, of results at least as extreme as those observed. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true and is not a measure of effect size.

sections.heading: Repeated analysis
sections.body: Multiple comparisons, data snooping, missing data and selecting only attractive results can distort conclusions. Report the method, assumptions, uncertainty and practical effect—not only a threshold.

title: Optimization: how models improve
summary: Compare gradient-based learning with broader search methods.

sections.heading: Objective and constraints
sections.body: An optimization problem states what to minimize or maximize and what constraints apply. A lower training loss is not always the best real-world outcome; choose an objective aligned with evaluation and risk.

sections.heading: Gradients and updates
sections.body: Backpropagation computes gradients using the chain rule. Gradient descent uses an update such as new weight = old weight − learning rate × gradient. Optimizers differ in how they choose and adjust updates.

sections.heading: Beyond gradients
sections.body: Evolutionary algorithms, simulated annealing and particle swarm optimization search through candidate solutions in different ways. They are not interchangeable, and no one method is best for every objective.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.body: Choose methods based on data, convergence, computational cost and whether derivatives are available. Hyperparameters such as learning rate and batch size need evaluation; a stationary point need not be a global optimum.

title: Safe AI agents and tool use
summary: Put boundaries around systems that retrieve information and take actions.

sections.heading: Separate language from authority
sections.body: An agent may choose tools or sequence tasks, but permissions must be enforced by the surrounding software. Define what actions are allowed, for whom and under what conditions.

sections.heading: Untrusted information
sections.body: A retrieved page, file or message may contain instructions intended to redirect an AI system. Treat it as data; validate tool inputs and outputs and restrict access to secrets and external actions.

sections.heading: Operate within limits
sections.body: Set time, cost and iteration limits. Use human approval for consequential actions where appropriate, preserve the ability to stop or roll back, and decide how failures should be surfaced.

sections.heading: Evaluate the whole workflow
sections.body: Test realistic abuse and failure cases, including tool misuse, stale information and compounded errors across agents. Record enough evidence for investigation while limiting sensitive data collection.

title: AI careers and a learning roadmap
summary: Explore the different roles behind an AI system and choose a practical next step.

sections.heading: Different roles, shared work
sections.body: Data engineers build and maintain data pipelines. Data analysts examine and communicate information. Data scientists investigate questions and build models; ML engineers focus on systems that train, deploy and operate models. Titles and responsibilities vary.

sections.heading: Build a foundation
sections.body: Develop comfort with programming, data handling, linear algebra and probability. Practice asking a focused question, cleaning data, building a baseline and explaining the result.

sections.heading: Make a small project
sections.body: Choose a problem with accessible data. Keep a held-out evaluation set, document limitations and show how a user would act on the result. A clear, reproducible small project can teach more than copying a large model.

sections.heading: Keep learning
sections.body: Read primary documentation, revisit assumptions and seek domain expertise. Career outcomes and demand vary by location and over time; the historical forecasts in the source material are not current predictions.

sections.heading: Read old employment forecasts as forecasts
sections.body: The World Economic Forum’s 2020 report estimated that a changing division of work between people and machines could displace 85 million jobs by 2025, while 97 million new roles might emerge. These were estimates from a particular historical report, not measured job losses or a current prediction. The underlying scope and assumptions matter.

title: A guide to common machine-learning models
summary: Compare regression, trees, nearest neighbors, clustering and dimensionality reduction.

sections.heading: Regression and classification
sections.body: Linear regression predicts a numerical response using a combination of features. Logistic regression models a class probability. Both need appropriate features, evaluation and attention to assumptions; correlation does not establish causation.

sections.heading: Trees and ensembles
sections.body: A decision tree makes a sequence of splits. Random forests combine multiple trees, often trained on resampled data and subsets of features. Boosting builds an ensemble sequentially to reduce a chosen loss; variants differ in their update rules.

sections.heading: Neighbors and boundaries
sections.body: K-nearest neighbors makes a prediction from similar training examples, so its notion of distance and feature scaling matter. A support vector machine finds a separating boundary; kernel methods can represent nonlinear relationships.

sections.heading: Grouping and compression
sections.body: K-means assigns points to clusters around centers; the number of clusters and distance measure are choices, not discovered facts. Principal component analysis finds directions of variation and can reduce dimensions, but high variance is not necessarily high predictive value.

title: Explore data before modeling
summary: Use visualization, sampling and context to understand a dataset.

sections.heading: Know where the data came from
sections.body: Structured data has an organized schema; text, images and other unstructured material may require additional processing. Record how data was collected, who is represented and whether its use is permitted.

sections.heading: Look at the distribution
sections.body: Use counts, histograms, boxplots and scatterplots alongside summary statistics. Check missing values, skew, outliers and inconsistent units. Averages can hide differences between groups.

sections.heading: Find patterns carefully
sections.body: Correlation measures association, not causation. A trend can change or reverse when groups are combined, as in Simpson’s paradox. Investigate potential confounders, collection changes and plausible alternatives.

sections.heading: Prepare without leaking
sections.body: Keep a separate evaluation set and fit preprocessing steps on the appropriate training split. For time series, use past data to predict later outcomes. Review duplicates and data that would not be available at prediction time.

title: Training neural networks in practice
summary: Understand losses, gradients, batches and common training techniques.

sections.heading: Forward pass and loss
sections.body: Inputs move through layers to produce an output. A loss measures discrepancy from a target or other objective; mean squared error and cross-entropy suit different tasks and assumptions.

sections.heading: Gradients and optimization
sections.body: Backpropagation applies the chain rule to calculate gradients of the loss with respect to parameters. An optimizer uses them to update parameters; the learning rate controls the scale of an update.

sections.heading: Batches and epochs
sections.body: A batch is a subset processed together. An epoch is one pass through the training dataset; the number of updates depends on batch size and how the final batch is handled.

sections.heading: Generalization techniques
sections.body: Validation data, early stopping, regularization, dropout and normalization can help training or generalization in different ways. A lower training loss or a small gradient alone does not guarantee good performance on unseen cases.

title: From images and words to shared representations
summary: Follow a simplified contrastive learning workflow for paired text and images.

sections.heading: Prepare pairs
sections.body: Start with images and associated text. The pairing quality matters: captions can be incomplete, biased or wrong.

sections.heading: Encode and compare
sections.body: Separate image and text encoders produce representations, which can be projected into a shared space. Similarity scores compare each image with candidate text descriptions.

sections.heading: Learn from matches
sections.body: A contrastive objective encourages corresponding pairs to score more highly than mismatched pairs. Batch construction and the loss affect what the representations learn.

sections.heading: Use and evaluate
sections.body: A system can compare a new image with candidate descriptions. Results are similarity-based predictions, not verified descriptions; test the intended task and relevant populations.
