title: Probability distributions: choose by the question
summary: Distinguish counts, waiting times, proportions, tails and multivariate models.

sections.heading: Discrete outcomes
sections.body: A Bernoulli variable represents a binary outcome with success probability p. A binomial variable counts successes in n independent trials with the same p. A categorical distribution selects one of several categories; a multinomial counts category outcomes over repeated trials. A degenerate distribution places all probability at one value.

sections.heading: Counts, waiting and sampling
sections.body: Poisson models count events under a specified rate model. Geometric distributions describe trials until a first success, with conventions differing on whether the successful trial is counted; negative binomial distributions extend the waiting-to-success idea. Hypergeometric models sampling without replacement. Wallenius’ noncentral hypergeometric distribution introduces biased sampling. Yule–Simon and zeta/Zipf models describe particular discrete heavy-tailed patterns.

sections.heading: Symmetric and bounded values
sections.body: A normal distribution is specified by a mean and variance. A uniform distribution assigns equal density over an interval. Beta and Kumaraswamy distributions describe flexible shapes on a bounded interval, commonly (0,1). A triangular distribution adds a mode between endpoints; a trapezoidal distribution has a flat central density region. A Laplace distribution has an exponential-shaped tail on either side of its center.

sections.heading: Positive values and waiting times
sections.body: The exponential distribution has a constant hazard and is memoryless. Weibull models can have increasing or decreasing hazard. Lognormal variables have normally distributed logarithms. Inverse Gaussian, Gompertz and Lindley distributions are other positive-variable families; suitability depends on the generating process and fit, not simply positive observations. Folded normal and half-normal distributions arise from absolute values of normal variables.

sections.heading: Heavy tails and extremes
sections.body: Cauchy is a heavy-tailed distribution whose mean and variance are undefined. Lévy, Pareto, stable, Burr and Fisk families provide different tail behavior. Generalized extreme-value models describe certain normalized maxima, and generalized error and Tukey lambda families allow flexible shapes. A power law is a functional tail pattern, not a universal explanation for a dataset.

sections.heading: Multiple dimensions and angles
sections.body: Bivariate and multivariate normal models describe joint variation. Dirichlet distributions model vectors of proportions; Wishart distributions are associated with covariance matrices. Von Mises and Kent distributions describe directional data in different spaces. Rayleigh, Rician and Nakagami models appear in magnitude and signal applications.

sections.heading: Families versus descriptions
sections.body: Skewed, symmetric, unimodal, bimodal, multimodal, long-tailed and U-shaped describe properties rather than identifying a unique distribution. A marginal comes from a joint distribution; a mixture combines component distributions. Truncation restricts support and requires renormalization. An empirical distribution assigns mass to observed data.

sections.heading: A count example
sections.body: If X is binomial with n = 3 and p = 0.5, then P(X=2) = C(3,2)×0.5²×0.5 = 3/8. This calculation requires independent trials with a common success probability.

sections.heading: Ambiguous names in the collection
sections.body: The labels “T Factorial”, “F J Shaped”, “G-and-H”, “Normal Lindley” and “Open Ended” need a precise definition or original reference before a formula can be assigned. “Inverse normal” may mean a quantile function or a named distribution depending on context; it should not automatically be equated with inverse Gaussian. These unresolved labels are retained in the editorial inventory.

title: Regression: fit, interpret and diagnose
summary: Move beyond fitting a line to checking assumptions, coding variables and measuring errors.

sections.heading: A complete line example
sections.body: For x = [0,1,2] and observed y = [1,2,2], the least-squares line is ŷ = 7/6 + x/2. Fitted values are [7/6,5/3,13/6] and residuals y−ŷ are [−1/6,1/3,−1/6]. Their squared sum is 1/6.

sections.heading: Separate error measures
sections.body: RMSE is √(SSE/n), approximately 0.2357 here. Residual standard error for this line with an intercept and slope is √(SSE/(n−2)), approximately 0.4082. They use different denominators. R² = 1−SSE/SST measures improvement over the mean baseline in this setting; out-of-sample R² can be negative.

sections.heading: Code features deliberately
sections.body: One-hot encoding represents categories with indicators. In an intercept-based linear model, a reference category or other constraint avoids redundant columns. Deviation coding compares levels with an overall effect under a defined convention. An interaction term lets one predictor’s association depend on another; a main effect is not a claim of independence.

sections.heading: Check stability and assumptions
sections.body: Collinear predictors can make coefficients unstable. Leverage concerns an observation’s predictor position, while influence concerns its effect on the fitted model. Examine residual patterns, changing variance (heteroskedasticity), dependence and unusual observations. Normality assumptions relate to particular inferential procedures, not a universal prerequisite for prediction.

sections.heading: Extend the model
sections.body: Polynomial terms and splines represent curves; knots locate spline transitions. Generalized additive models combine smooth effects. Lasso penalizes coefficient magnitudes, Bayesian regression uses a prior, quantile regression targets conditional quantiles, and robust regression reduces sensitivity under chosen loss rules. These approaches answer different questions.

sections.heading: Validate outside the fitting data
sections.body: Cross-validation rotates training and validation folds, but the split must respect groups and time. Fit scaling and feature selection within the training portion. Use weighted regression only when the weight meaning is justified.

title: Experiments, uncertainty and evaluation formulas
summary: Work through a confusion matrix, sampling uncertainty and the logic of testing.

sections.heading: Calculate a confusion matrix
sections.body: Suppose TP=8, FP=2, FN=4 and TN=86. Accuracy is 94/100 = 94%; precision is 8/10 = 80%; recall is 8/12 ≈ 66.7%; specificity is 86/88 ≈ 97.7%. F1 = 2TP/(2TP+FP+FN) = 16/22 ≈ 72.7%. The same model can look strong or weak depending on the error that matters.

sections.heading: Change the threshold
sections.body: A threshold converts a score into a decision. ROC plots true-positive rate against false-positive rate across thresholds; a precision–recall curve focuses on predicted and actual positives. AUC summarizes a curve and does not choose the right operating threshold for a business.

sections.heading: Sampling uncertainty
sections.body: For independent observations with sample standard deviation s, the estimated standard error of the mean is s/√n. A central limit theorem can justify an approximation under its conditions; it does not make the original observations normally distributed. Bootstrap resampling draws samples with replacement from observed data and has its own limitations.

sections.heading: Design the comparison
sections.body: Random assignment allocates subjects to treatment and control; random sampling selects observations from a population. They solve different problems. Define effect size, statistical power and the analysis before examining results where possible.

sections.heading: Choose an appropriate test
sections.body: A t-test concerns means under specified assumptions; ANOVA compares modelled group effects using an F statistic. Chi-square procedures can compare categorical counts, and permutation tests use an exchangeability argument. Pairwise and omnibus tests answer different questions.

sections.heading: Interpret errors and multiple tests
sections.body: A Type I error rejects a true null; a Type II error fails to reject a false null under an alternative. Alpha controls a test’s Type I error rate under its assumptions. False discovery rate concerns the expected proportion of false rejections among rejections, with conventions for no rejections. Multiple testing needs an appropriate procedure rather than reusing an unadjusted threshold.

title: Search and optimization methods: a field guide
summary: Understand the mechanism behind search methods and distinguish algorithm names from settings.

sections.heading: Gradient and curvature methods
sections.body: BFGS is a quasi-Newton method that builds a curvature approximation. Rprop uses gradient signs to adapt update steps; momentum carries a running influence of previous gradients. KKT conditions combine stationarity, feasibility and complementary slackness under specified conditions; they are not a blanket proof of global optimality.

sections.heading: Evolutionary search
sections.body: Genetic algorithms select, recombine and mutate candidate representations. Genetic programming evolves program structures. Differential evolution perturbs candidates using differences between population members. Estimation-of-distribution algorithms learn a probabilistic model of promising candidates and sample from it.

sections.heading: Collective search
sections.body: Particle swarm optimization updates candidate positions using individual and collective information. Ant-colony methods maintain pheromone-like search information, often for combinatorial problems. Artificial bee colony and the bees algorithm allocate exploration among candidate regions; they are distinct methods despite similar metaphors.

sections.heading: Memory and neighborhoods
sections.body: Tabu search uses memory to restrict selected moves. Variable neighborhood search changes neighborhood structures to escape local patterns. Simulated annealing can accept worse candidates according to a temperature schedule. Shuffled frog leaping combines local improvement with regrouping of candidates.

sections.heading: Other named metaheuristics
sections.body: Cuckoo search, firefly algorithms, gravitational search, imperialist competition and cultural algorithms define different population-update mechanisms. Their biological or social metaphors do not establish performance. Compare a specific implementation with simple baselines under the same evaluation budget.

sections.heading: Harmony search settings
sections.body: Harmony search builds candidates using stored solutions, random choices and adjustments. Harmony memory considering rate is commonly a parameter governing memory use; it should not be listed as a standalone optimizer. The source’s “Harmony Memory Upgrade” label needs an original reference to establish its intended meaning.

sections.heading: A fair comparison
sections.body: State the objective, constraints, variable encoding, stopping rule, random seeds and compute budget. Run multiple trials for stochastic methods and report distributions of outcomes, not only the best run.

title: Image features: edges, corners, blobs and descriptors
summary: Organize classical computer-vision methods by what they detect or describe.

sections.heading: Edges and derivatives
sections.body: Sobel, Prewitt and Roberts operators approximate image derivatives. Canny combines smoothing, gradient information and further processing to produce edges. Deriche filters offer another approach. An edge marks an intensity change, which need not coincide with an object boundary.

sections.heading: Corners and local structure
sections.body: Harris and Shi–Tomasi use local gradient structure to identify informative points. A structure tensor summarizes variation in different directions; points with variation in more than one direction can be useful for tracking and matching.

sections.heading: Scale and regions
sections.body: Laplacian-of-Gaussian, Difference-of-Gaussians and Hessian-based methods detect structures over scale. Maximally stable extremal regions identify stable image regions across thresholds. Image pyramids support multiscale processing. Scale-space methods explain how representations change with smoothing.

sections.heading: Shapes and invariance
sections.body: Hough transforms accumulate evidence for parameterized shapes; a generalized Hough transform handles more general templates. Affine-adapted region methods aim to improve matching under viewpoint changes. These methods have assumptions and can fail under occlusion, noise or repeated textures.

sections.heading: Descriptors
sections.body: SIFT, SURF and GLOH summarize local visual structure for comparison. HOG describes gradient orientations, local binary patterns encode local intensity comparisons, and GIST summarizes scene-level structure. A descriptor is different from a detector: one describes a region while the other finds candidate regions.

sections.heading: Choose by the task
sections.body: Tracking, image matching, classification and segmentation need different outputs. Evaluate repeatability, robustness, compute cost and any licensing or patent constraints for the intended implementation. The source’s PCBR abbreviation requires its original reference before a specific algorithm can be described.

title: Business analytics and scenario planning
summary: Distinguish describing results, predicting outcomes and exploring uncertain futures.

sections.heading: Start with the decision
sections.body: Aggregate analysis summarizes populations or segments; trend analysis follows change over time; segmentation groups cases for a stated purpose. A descriptive relationship does not prove what will happen if a business intervenes.

sections.heading: Estimate with transparent assumptions
sections.body: For a hypothetical market with 10,000 eligible customers, 20% adoption and 50 units of annual revenue per adopter, the estimate is 100,000 units. If adoption ranges from 10% to 30%, the result ranges from 50,000 to 150,000. These are scenario assumptions, not observed outcomes.

sections.heading: Triangulate
sections.body: Approach an estimate using another model or independent evidence. Agreement is more useful when the methods do not share the same hidden assumptions. Record uncertainty in the inputs instead of disguising it with precise output formatting.

sections.heading: Map plausible futures
sections.body: Scenario planning examines multiple plausible futures rather than assigning certainty to one forecast. Cognitive maps represent perceived relationships; fuzzy cognitive maps add weighted influences and update rules. Their results depend on elicitation, weights and assumptions.

sections.heading: Use experts carefully
sections.body: Delphi-style exercises gather and revise expert judgments; scenario workshops can incorporate stakeholder perspectives and identify disagreements. The source’s specific scenario counts and expert-count recommendations lack cited evidence and are not treated as fixed requirements.

sections.heading: Close the loop
sections.body: State the decision, monitor signals that distinguish scenarios and revise assumptions as evidence arrives. A useful scenario changes what the team is prepared to do, rather than only producing a presentation.

title: Clustering, distances and representation learning
summary: Compare ways to group observations, measure similarity and reduce dimensions.

sections.heading: Distances encode assumptions
sections.body: Euclidean distance is √Σ(xᵢ−yᵢ)²; Manhattan distance is Σ|xᵢ−yᵢ|. Hamming distance counts mismatched positions rather than summing signed differences. Feature scaling can change which observations are nearest. Gower-style dissimilarity combines feature-specific comparisons for mixed data; it is not simply min–max scaling.

sections.heading: Hierarchies and mixtures
sections.body: Agglomerative clustering merges groups; divisive clustering splits them. A dendrogram records a hierarchy under a chosen distance and linkage. Gaussian mixture models represent data as weighted component distributions and can provide soft assignments. Expectation-maximization alternates estimating latent assignments and updating parameters; convergence need not identify the globally best fit.

sections.heading: Choose complexity
sections.body: AIC and BIC balance likelihood with complexity under different criteria. They are not substitutes for checking assumptions or validating a downstream task. Clusters may be useful even when they do not correspond to stable human categories.

sections.heading: Find lower-dimensional structure
sections.body: PCA uses orthogonal directions of variance; loadings describe the transformation and a scree plot shows explained variance. SVD factorizes a matrix and underlies many low-rank approximations. Alternating least squares optimizes factor matrices one at a time.

sections.heading: Nonlinear embeddings
sections.body: Locally linear embedding, Isomap, multidimensional scaling and t-SNE use different objectives to preserve aspects of structure. A visually separated plot does not establish that true distinct populations exist; neighborhood, scale and parameter choices matter.

sections.heading: Learn representations
sections.body: An autoencoder learns an encoding through reconstruction. Contrastive learning learns representations using positive and negative relationships. A self-organizing map moves a winning prototype and nearby map prototypes toward an observation: w′ = w + αh(x−w). Its map topology and distance choices shape the result.

title: Trees, ensembles and feature importance
summary: Understand split criteria, pruning, bagging and boosting with an impurity calculation.

sections.heading: From a split to a prediction
sections.body: A tree divides records using feature conditions. Internal nodes choose tests, branches apply outcomes and leaves hold predictions. Recursive partitioning stops under a rule such as minimum leaf size or maximum depth; it need not make every leaf pure.

sections.heading: Calculate impurity
sections.body: For class proportions [0.75,0.25], Gini impurity is 1−(0.75²+0.25²)=0.375. Binary entropy in bits is −0.75 log₂(0.75)−0.25 log₂(0.25)≈0.8113. The source omitted the square in its Gini formula; 1−Σp would always be zero for a complete distribution.

sections.heading: Bagging and random forests
sections.body: Bagging fits models to bootstrap samples and combines outputs. Random forests add feature randomization when building trees. Averaging can reduce variance, but it does not make biased data representative.

sections.heading: Boosting variants
sections.body: AdaBoost changes example weights according to classification errors. Gradient boosting fits successive learners to improve a differentiable loss, often through negative gradients. Stochastic variants sample observations or features. XGBoost is a software system with its own objectives and implementation choices, not a synonym for every boosting method.

sections.heading: Interpret with care
sections.body: Impurity-based importance can favor certain features; permutation importance measures the effect of shuffling under a chosen evaluation. Correlated features can share or hide importance. Neither measure alone proves causality.

sections.heading: Select features without leakage
sections.body: Forward selection, chi-square-based screening and other selection procedures must be fitted within training folds. Association rules describe co-occurrence: support measures frequency and confidence estimates a conditional proportion; neither establishes causal influence.

title: Time series, hidden states and forecasting
summary: Connect probabilistic sequence models, filtering and time-aware evaluation.

sections.heading: State and observations
sections.body: A Markov model describes a transition law with a stated dependence structure. A hidden Markov model adds unobserved states that emit observations. A Kalman filter estimates a state in a linear Gaussian setting by alternating prediction and observation updates; extensions relax some assumptions.

sections.heading: Smoothing and transformation
sections.body: Moving averages and exponential smoothing aggregate past observations using different weight patterns. A random walk is a stochastic model and may be a useful forecasting baseline; it is not itself a general noise-removal algorithm. Fourier and wavelet transforms represent signals in frequency- or scale-related bases.

sections.heading: Dependence and stationarity
sections.body: Autocorrelation measures relationships between a series and lagged versions. Ljung–Box and Box–Pierce Q statistics assess collections of autocorrelations under assumptions. Dickey–Fuller tests concern a unit-root null, rather than simply whether financial data changes. A Hurst-exponent estimate depends on method and sample properties.

sections.heading: Validate in time order
sections.body: Train on data available at the forecast origin and evaluate on later observations. Repeated random splits can leak future information. Compare with naive or seasonal baselines and examine different horizons and changing regimes.

sections.heading: Financial-model claims
sections.body: OHLCV features, technical indicators and neural networks can be inputs to an experiment, but their presence does not establish a profitable strategy. Include costs, slippage, data revisions and multiple-model selection. The supplied return and Sharpe figures lack dates, data, methodology and cost assumptions, so they cannot substantiate performance.

sections.heading: Sampling versus filtering
sections.body: Markov chain Monte Carlo constructs a chain for sampling a target distribution. It serves a different purpose from state estimation in a Kalman filter, despite both using probabilistic transitions.

title: How model complexity affects time and memory
summary: Read complexity expressions with the algorithm, data layout and hardware assumptions attached.

sections.heading: Define the workload
sections.body: Let n be observations, p features, T trees, I iterations, k clusters and d tree depth. Training and prediction are different workloads. Big-O describes asymptotic growth under a model of computation, not a benchmark or a latency guarantee.

sections.heading: Linear models and neighbors
sections.body: A dense least-squares solve using normal-equation-style operations can cost O(np²+p³); iterative methods have different costs and numerical behavior. Logistic regression needs iterative optimization, so O(np) may describe a pass rather than total training. Brute-force nearest-neighbor prediction scans O(np) values; storing or indexing observations is not literally free training.

sections.heading: Trees and ensembles
sections.body: A tree prediction follows a path of depth d. An ensemble of T trees costs roughly O(Td) per example apart from feature access and overhead. Training complexity depends on the split search, sorting, sparsity and tree construction; a fixed O(n log n p) expression is not universal.

sections.heading: Clusters and components
sections.body: A straightforward k-means assignment/update run costs roughly O(Inkp). PCA cost depends on whether a full SVD, eigensolve or randomized approximation is used and on the relative dimensions. A reduced projection to m components typically multiplies a p-dimensional input by a p×m matrix.

sections.heading: Neural-network cost
sections.body: A dense transformation with p inputs and h outputs performs work proportional to ph per example. Total training additionally depends on layers, examples, update steps, activation storage and optimizer state. A sparse mixture-of-experts model separates total parameters from parameters activated per token.

sections.heading: Measure the actual system
sections.body: Report hardware, batch size, sequence length, precision, concurrency, warm-up and memory use. Accelerator utilization, network calls and data loading may dominate a simple operation count.

title: Activations and less familiar network families
summary: Use correct activation formulas and distinguish network families from named implementations.

sections.heading: Activation formulas
sections.body: Sigmoid(z)=1/(1+exp(−z)); tanh(z)=(exp(z)−exp(−z))/(exp(z)+exp(−z)); ReLU(z)=max(0,z). The source expression 1−tanh²(z) is the derivative of tanh, not tanh itself. A threshold maps a score to discrete outcomes; sigmoid alone produces a continuous value.

sections.heading: Variants and learned behavior
sections.body: Leaky ReLU uses max(αz,z) for a chosen small positive α; the source mixes α=0.01 and α=0.1, so a value must be stated. ELU uses a negative exponential branch. Maxout selects the maximum of learned affine responses. Softmax normalizes a vector rather than independently squashing each component.

sections.heading: Recurrent families
sections.body: LSTMs use cell-state and gate operations; a commonly written output is hₜ=oₜ⊙tanh(cₜ). GRUs blend a candidate and previous hidden state using gates, with conventions differing between descriptions. Elman and Jordan networks feed back different signals; continuous-time RNNs use a continuous-time evolution rule.

sections.heading: Convolutions and other structures
sections.body: A convolutional network learns local filters. Max pooling selects maxima while average pooling averages regions. AlexNet, VGG, ResNet, Inception and Xception name architectures, not datasets. CIFAR names datasets. Capsule networks use a different representational design; they are not a universal successor to CNNs.

sections.heading: Specialized architectures
sections.body: Radial basis function networks use functions depending on distance to a center, such as exp(−(εr)²). Φ is a function symbol here, not the golden ratio. Modular networks divide processing among parts. Highway networks gate information paths; Network-in-Network uses local learned submodels, and deep supervision adds training objectives at intermediate layers.

sections.heading: Energy and belief models
sections.body: Energy-based models assign relative compatibility through an energy function; this does not imply electrical-spike hardware. Restricted Boltzmann machines have visible and hidden units with a restricted connection structure. Contrastive divergence approximates aspects of their training. Deep belief networks and neuromorphic systems are distinct ideas; the source’s expected-signal-propagation label needs its particular reference before further claims are made.

title: Design an agent platform from tools to operations
summary: Place tools, memory, protocols and execution controls in the parts of a system that own them.

sections.heading: Application and execution
sections.body: Assistants, researchers, scheduling agents and content tools are applications. Their execution layer coordinates tasks and tool calls, records state and handles retries. Planning text is not the same as executing an authorized action.

sections.heading: Memory and knowledge
sections.body: Working context, conversation history, preferences and durable memories have different lifetimes and privacy implications. Retrieval can use a search index, vector store or knowledge graph. An ontology describes concepts and relationships; storing embeddings alone does not create one. FAISS is a similarity-search library, not a hosted database service.

sections.heading: Tools and protocols
sections.body: A tool interface describes an operation, inputs and outputs. Model Context Protocol standardizes aspects of connecting applications with tools and context; A2A addresses agent interoperability. Identity, authorization, validation and isolation still require implementation. The source’s ACP, ANP, AGORA, AGP, TAP, OAP and FCP labels are not assumed to denote unique interoperable standards without the exact specification.

sections.heading: Framework choices
sections.body: LangGraph supports stateful graph-based workflows, LangChain offers tools for model-backed applications, CrewAI organizes agent/task workflows, and AutoGen supports agentic applications with its own architecture. Compare the current documentation against required control, state, human review and deployment needs instead of assuming every project needs all four.

sections.heading: Infrastructure and observability
sections.body: HTTP, WebSockets, storage, data pipelines, accelerators, load balancers and CDNs support different parts of the system. Track latency, failures, cost and task outcomes across model and tool calls. Logs should expose enough information for diagnosis while minimizing private content.

sections.heading: Operate deliberately
sections.body: A registry can record owners, permissions and versions. Quotas and budgets bound resource use. Execution sandboxes and policy enforcement constrain tools. A no-code builder changes how workflows are authored; it does not remove the need to evaluate permissions and failures.

title: Language-model labels: architecture, size and capability
summary: Understand which labels describe a technical structure and which describe a product goal.

sections.heading: Overlapping descriptions
sections.body: GPT usually expands to generative pretrained transformer. “Small language model” is a relative size description; “vision-language model” describes modalities. A single system can be small, multimodal and transformer-based at the same time.

sections.heading: Architecture labels
sections.body: Mixture of experts describes routing through expert modules. A dense transformer and an MoE transformer can both generate language. These labels do not specify accuracy, source grounding or permission to act.

sections.heading: Reasoning and action
sections.body: Reasoning-model and action-model labels describe goals or capabilities more than one universal architecture. Producing a reasoning trace or self-check does not guarantee that the reasoning is faithful or the answer correct. An action-capable system still needs tool permissions and execution controls.

sections.heading: Research-specific models
sections.body: Hierarchical Reasoning Model and Large Concept Model refer to particular research designs. Their high/low-level recurrence or concept-embedding generation should be read against the original research, rather than treated as mandatory steps for all language models.

sections.heading: Choose based on a task
sections.body: Evaluate the inputs, outputs, quality, latency, compute cost, context handling and permitted uses. A collection of acronyms is not a ranking of model capability.

title: AI, cognition and symbolic reasoning
summary: Separate useful computational ideas from claims that machines think like people.

sections.heading: Rules and representations
sections.body: Symbolic systems represent facts and relations explicitly and apply rules or search. Expert systems combine a knowledge base and inference procedures. Automated reasoning, planning and scheduling solve specified logical or decision problems; they need not learn from examples.

sections.heading: Reason with uncertainty
sections.body: Fuzzy logic represents graded membership in a set, which differs from a probability of an event. Probabilistic models represent uncertainty under a specified model. A hybrid system can combine learned representations with explicit rules or constraints.

sections.heading: Brains as an analogy
sections.body: A network’s nodes and weights are mathematical objects. Comparing them with neurons, dendrites and synapses can be a teaching analogy but does not establish biological equivalence. Human working, episodic, semantic and procedural memory do not map one-to-one to an agent’s database tables. Biomimicry borrows ideas from biological systems to solve engineering problems; biological inspiration alone does not demonstrate equivalent cognition.

sections.heading: Tests and intelligence
sections.body: Turing’s imitation-game proposal concerns behavior in an interaction. Lovelace-style tests concern creative output under defined criteria. Psychometric g and proposed multiple-intelligence categories concern theories and measurements of people; they are not interchangeable machine benchmarks.

sections.heading: Arguments and limits
sections.body: Speed alone does not establish general intelligence, and humanlike behavior is not the only possible criterion. Computational complexity can make some problems expensive even for capable systems. The supplied “fast-thinking dog” and other named arguments lack enough context to reconstruct their original premises.

sections.heading: Speculation versus evidence
sections.body: Quantum hardware does not by itself establish consciousness, human-level reasoning or unlimited intelligence. Claims about sentience, motivation or superintelligence require a definition and evidence; colorful analogies in the source are not scientific findings.

sections.heading: Names whose premises are missing
sections.body: The collection lists the fast-thinking dog, anthropocentric, limits-of-intelligence and computational-complexity arguments without their original sources or complete premises. The guide explains speed, human comparisons and computational limits, but cannot reconstruct a specific author’s argument from those names alone.

title: Adopting AI: people, value and decision rights
summary: Connect an AI use case to ownership, measurable value and how work changes.

sections.heading: Build a use-case portfolio
sections.body: State the expected benefit, affected users, baseline cost and failure consequences. Estimate inference, tool, review, integration and maintenance costs. Automation does not imply zero marginal cost.

sections.heading: Define authority
sections.body: Specify which decisions an agent may propose and which it may execute. Assign a human owner and escalation path. “Humans above the loop” is an operating-model phrase, not a reason to remove meaningful oversight.

sections.heading: Support people
sections.body: Provide role-specific training and opportunities to practice judging model outputs. Keep routes for challenging automated decisions. Fear of displacement, overtrust, changed responsibilities and loss of apprenticeship can affect adoption.

sections.heading: Use a shared platform deliberately
sections.body: Reusable identity, permissions, evaluation, observability and knowledge access can reduce duplicated work. An agent registry or orchestration layer earns its place when it solves an actual coordination need.

sections.heading: Measure outcomes
sections.body: Track task completion, quality, user harm, cost and the value produced. A successful demonstration or a high model score does not prove a business return. Revisit assumptions and stop uses whose costs or risks exceed their benefits.

title: AI governance frameworks: law, guidance and standards
summary: Distinguish legal obligations, voluntary risk frameworks and management-system certification.

sections.heading: Start with scope
sections.body: Identify the system’s purpose, parties, jurisdictions and deployment context. The source’s single deadline and four-tier summary cannot determine every obligation. Classification, exceptions and application dates must be checked in the applicable law.

sections.heading: EU AI Act
sections.body: The Act includes prohibited practices, high-risk-system obligations and transparency provisions under specific conditions. Not every fraud detector or trading model is automatically high risk, and low-risk uses are not exempt from all other laws. Penalties depend on the provision, party and applicable rules; the source’s simplified penalty chart is not a compliance calculator.

sections.heading: NIST AI RMF
sections.body: The framework organizes activities as Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. It is voluntary guidance; procurement or contractual requirements may refer to it in particular settings. The source’s claim that it is universally mandatory for enterprise procurement is not established.

sections.heading: ISO/IEC 42001
sections.body: This standard concerns an organizational AI management system, including policies, objectives and continual improvement. Certification can provide evidence about the management system within its scope; it does not guarantee every model output or replace legal obligations. Certification timing is organization-specific.

sections.heading: Singapore agentic guidance
sections.body: IMDA launched its Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI in January 2026. It addresses practices for responsible agent deployment. The source’s claims that every audit trail or autonomy classification is legally mandatory cannot be inferred simply from the existence of this framework.

sections.heading: Turn governance into work
sections.body: Inventory systems and tools; assess impacts and permissions; assign owners; record intended uses, limitations and controls; monitor results; and define review and response procedures. Choose review frequency based on risk and change rather than presenting a universal quarterly rule.

title: AI history: milestones and how to read the claims
summary: Distinguish dated milestones from broad claims about invention, intelligence and impact.

sections.heading: Foundations and research methods
sections.body: McCulloch and Pitts’ 1943 work formalized aspects of neural activity; Turing’s 1950 paper proposed an imitation-game discussion. The 1956 Dartmouth project helped establish AI as a named research field. These milestones do not imply a single invention date for every underlying idea.

sections.heading: Programs, products and dates
sections.body: The collection also names SNARC, General Problem Solver, ELIZA, Roomba, DeepFace and AlphaZero. They represent research hardware, problem-solving software, conversation, consumer robotics and specialized learning systems. The Computer History Museum dates Weizenbaum’s completed ELIZA to 1966; the source’s 1965 entry and several asserted firsts require that distinction. IBM’s Deep Blue match victory was in 1997 and Watson’s Jeopardy demonstration in 2011. A specialized result does not establish general intelligence.

sections.heading: Learning and evaluation
sections.body: Perceptron research explored learned decision rules. Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams’ 1986 paper demonstrated learning internal representations through backpropagation; it was not the first discovery of every form of gradient propagation. Expert systems and periods of reduced funding also form part of the history.

sections.heading: Games and scientific prediction
sections.body: DeepMind’s AlphaGo defeated Fan Hui in 2015 and Lee Sedol in March 2016; the source conflates these matches. AlphaFold’s CASP14 result was in 2020, with major published work in 2021. Protein structure prediction does not solve every problem of folding dynamics or biology.

sections.heading: Language models and public debate
sections.body: GPT-3 research appeared in 2020. Public controversies over sentience and copyright reflect social, legal and scientific debates; a claim or lawsuit does not establish its underlying allegation. The source’s names, dates and asserted firsts need primary records for more detailed historical treatment.

sections.heading: Claims that need context
sections.body: The source’s cat-recognition story attributes a 2012 result to the wrong research group; it should be checked against the original large-scale unsupervised-learning paper. Hardware acquisition prices, specific employment forecasts and an electricity-use infographic are historical or context-dependent facts, not reliable current statistics without their original source and denominator.

title: AI risk register: failure modes and controls
summary: Explore model, data, security, operational and human risks, with practical control questions.

sections.heading: Use the register in context
sections.body: Choose the risks relevant to a particular system and affected people, identify an owner and record evidence for the controls. The list is a starting point rather than an exhaustive or legally sufficient assessment.

sections.heading: Prioritize consequences
sections.body: Assess likelihood, exposure and the consequence of failure. A small model error can be serious when it triggers an action; a high aggregate score can conceal harmful outcomes for a subgroup.

title: Preprocessing, missing data and useful transformations
summary: Make transformations explicit and distinguish missingness assumptions from convenient fixes.

sections.heading: Scale for a reason
sections.body: Standardization typically subtracts a training mean and divides by a training standard deviation. Min–max scaling uses a defined range; rank transforms replace values with order-related information. Normalization is an overloaded word, so state the exact operation and handle constant features.

sections.heading: Describe missingness
sections.body: MCAR means missingness does not depend on observed or unobserved data under the model; MAR allows dependence on observed information; MNAR permits dependence on unobserved values after conditioning on observed data. A spreadsheet alone generally cannot establish which mechanism holds.

sections.heading: Impute within the workflow
sections.body: Dropping records, adding missingness indicators and imputing values make different assumptions. Fit imputers using the training portion of each split. Compare sensitivity to plausible missingness mechanisms and avoid presenting imputed values as observed facts.

sections.heading: Transform skew carefully
sections.body: Logarithms require positive inputs unless a defined alternative transform is used. Square-root and reciprocal transformations change scale and interpretation. Squaring values or applying a negative logarithm is not a universal cure for negative skew. Choose a transformation for the analysis and check its consequences.

sections.heading: Separate observations from summaries
sections.body: A sample statistic summarizes observations; a sampling distribution describes the statistic across repetitions. A z-score standardizes an observation under stated mean and spread. A QQ plot compares quantiles with another distribution and can expose departures hidden by a histogram.

sections.heading: Visualize the question
sections.body: A frequency table counts observations in categories or intervals; a histogram displays binned numeric counts, while a density estimate smooths an estimated distribution. Violin plots combine a density view with summaries. Hexagonal binning and contour plots summarize bivariate density; neither is automatically more informative than plotting points.

sections.heading: Evaluate residuals and associations
sections.body: Mean error can hide positive and negative cancellation; MAE and RMSE measure error size differently. Pearson correlation concerns linear association and may be undefined for constant variables. Contingency tables summarize categorical counts. Theil’s uncertainty coefficient is an entropy-based association measure; the same name also appears in different forecasting statistics, so specify the definition.

title: Language, perception and embodied AI
summary: Connect language tasks, sensory inputs, symbolic knowledge and real-world applications.

sections.heading: Language tasks
sections.body: Text classification assigns labels; named-entity recognition identifies spans such as organization or person names; translation maps between languages; summarization condenses content. Sequence-to-sequence models produce an output sequence from an input sequence, with architecture and training varying by task.

sections.heading: Sentence representations
sections.body: Sentence encoders such as the historical skip-thought approach learn representations intended to capture information beyond individual words. Modern embeddings also vary by task and training objective; a vector’s usefulness should be evaluated for the intended retrieval or classification problem.

sections.heading: Speech, sensors and robotics
sections.body: Speech recognition converts audio into text or related representations. Robotics combines perception, state estimation, planning and control with physical constraints. Sensor fusion combines information sources; errors and delays can propagate into real-world actions.

sections.heading: Edge, cloud and ubiquitous computing
sections.body: Edge computing processes information near its source, while cloud systems use remote infrastructure. Edge AI can reduce communication needs but faces device limits. Internet-of-Things systems connect devices and data; ubiquitous computing concerns computing integrated into everyday environments. These are deployment concepts, not model architectures.

sections.heading: Knowledge and interaction
sections.body: Knowledge bases and graphs can encode explicit relationships. Human–computer interaction examines how people use and understand systems. A conversational interface, a symbolic planner and a learned perception model can coexist without being interchangeable.

sections.heading: Application limits
sections.body: Healthcare, finance and autonomous systems have different evidence and oversight needs. Demonstrating a model on a benchmark does not establish clinical benefit, trading profit or operational safety. Validate the system where it will actually be used.

sections.heading: Unidentified model name
sections.body: The supplied “Text-guided Attention Model” fragment associates images with generated language, but gives no paper, architecture or version. Image captioning and text-conditioned visual attention are useful task descriptions; the fragment is insufficient to identify a particular model.

title: Cloud data pipelines: roles before product names
summary: Read a cloud architecture by what each stage does, and recognize outdated or misplaced service labels.

sections.heading: A reusable pipeline
sections.body: Separate ingestion, durable storage, processing, serving and visualization. An event stream, object archive, relational database and model endpoint have different roles even when one provider supplies all of them.

sections.heading: AWS examples in the collection
sections.body: The source names IoT, Lambda, Kinesis streams, S3 and Glacier, EMR, Glue, SageMaker, Redshift, RDS, Elasticsearch, DynamoDB, Athena and QuickSight. These span ingestion, compute, storage, analytics and visualization; the arrows in the drawing are not proof of configured or required integrations. The former Kinesis Data Analytics name must be read against current Managed Service for Apache Flink documentation.

sections.heading: Azure examples in the collection
sections.body: IoT Hub, Functions, Event Hubs, Data Lake storage, Data Explorer, Databricks, Stream Analytics, Azure SQL, Cosmos DB, Redis, Azure ML and Power BI occupy different parts of an architecture. Product generations, names and availability need current documentation when implementing a system.

sections.heading: Correct the Google Cloud drawing
sections.body: The supplied Google Cloud diagram contains an Azure Data Lake Store label and a Power BI destination; those are not native Google Cloud service names. Its historical Cloud IoT label also needs context: IoT Core was discontinued in August 2023. Pub/Sub, Dataproc, Dataflow, BigQuery, Bigtable, Cloud SQL and other labels should be evaluated for their actual roles rather than copied as a ready-made stack.

sections.heading: Choose an architecture
sections.body: Specify data volume, update rate, latency, permissions, durability, regions, recovery and operational ownership. Check whether a simpler managed workflow or existing storage already solves the requirement. Avoid buying every box in a reference diagram.

title: Measure AI energy use with context
summary: Distinguish model workloads, data-center electricity and emissions before comparing figures.

sections.heading: State the quantity
sections.body: Energy is accumulated consumption, commonly measured in kWh; power is a rate, commonly measured in kW. A data-center market’s total electricity consumption does not establish how much was used specifically for AI.

sections.heading: Define the workload
sections.body: Training, fine-tuning and inference have different patterns. Report model, hardware, utilization, batch size, sequence length, runtime and system scope. A per-request estimate depends on these assumptions and the method of allocation.

sections.heading: Separate energy from emissions
sections.body: Carbon emissions depend on electricity generation and the accounting method as well as consumption. Cooling and other facility overhead may also matter. A figure without a location, period, scope or denominator is difficult to compare responsibly.

sections.heading: Read the source infographic
sections.body: The supplied 2024 data-center-market infographic is retained as a historical source image. Its provenance, measurement method and underlying dataset were not provided. Its city values cannot substantiate current AI electricity use, so this guide explains how such a claim should be evaluated instead of reprinting the map as evidence.

Strategy is the direction and scope of an organisation over the long term: ideally, which matches its resources to its changing environment, and in particular its markets, customers or clients so as to meet stakeholder expectations. (Johnson & Scholes)
What business strategy is all about is, in a word, competitive advantage... The sole purposes of strategic planning is to enable a company to gain, as efficiently as possible, a sustainable edge over its competitors. (Kenichi Ohmae)
Strategy is a deliberate search for a plan of action that will develop a business’s competitive advantage and compound it. For any company, the search is an iterative process that begins with a recognition of where you are now and what you have now. Your most dangerous competitors are those that are most like you. sections.heading: What critical success factors mean
sections.body:
Critical Success Factors (CSFs)
An industry critical success factors (CSF) are those things that most affect the ability of industry members to prosper in the marketplace.
Critical success factors are those factors that are either particularly valued by customers or which provide a significant advantage in terms of cost.
Different industries and markets will have different critical success factors (e.g. in low-cost airlines the CSFs will be punctuality and value for money whereas in full-service airlines it is all about quality of service).
CSF concern what every industry must be competent at doing or concentrate on achieving in order to be competitively and financially successful – they are therefore the prerequisites for industry success.
Critical success factors are likely to be an important source of competitive advantage if an organisation has them (or a disadvantage if an organisation lacks them).
Critical Success Factors vary from industry to industry and even from time to time within the same industry as driving forces and competitive conditions change.

title: NLP language patterns: clarify assumptions and missing detail
summary: Explore the source’s meta-model terms, examples, clarifying questions, metaphors and indirect-language descriptions.

sections.heading: Generalization, deletion, distortion and example questions
sections.body:
The NLP Meta-Model
A set of language patterns used to challenge vague or distorted statements, clarify meaning, and uncover deeper thought processes by questioning generalizations, deletions, and distortions in language.
Generalisation
A cognitive process where one experience is applied broadly to other similar situations, which can be useful (e.g., learning) or limiting (e.g., “I failed once, so I always fail”).
Universal Quantifiers
Words like always, never, everyone, or no one that assume something applies in all cases, often leading to limiting beliefs.
Example: “I always mess things up.”
Lost Performative
A judgment or opinion stated without revealing who is making the judgment.
Example: “That’s a bad idea.”
(Who says so?)
Moral Operator
Words like should, must, have to, or ought to that imply obligation, often without clear reasoning.
Example: “You must work harder.”
(Says who? Why?)
Deletions
When part of the information is left out, making the statement vague or incomplete.
Example: “I’m unhappy.”
(About what? With whom?)
Lack of Referential Index
A vague statement with no specific subject or reference point.
Example: “They say it’s wrong.”
(Who is they?)
Comparative Deletion
A comparison is made, but what's being compared to is missing.
Example: “This is better.”
(Better than what?)
Distortions
When reality is misrepresented or reshaped in our language or thoughts—turning assumptions or internal beliefs into “truths.”
(This is the broad category that includes the rest of the terms below.)
Nominalisations
Turning processes or actions into static “things,” often abstract and vague.
Example: “There’s no communication.”
(‘Communication’ is a process, not a thing.)
Question: “How specifically is someone not communicating?”
Mind Reading
Assuming you know what someone else is thinking or feeling without evidence.
Example: “She hates me.”
Question: “How do you know that?”
Cause and Effect Distortion
Assuming one thing automatically causes another, especially in relationships or emotions.
Example: “You make me feel bad.”
Question: “How does what I do cause that feeling?”
Presuppositions
Hidden assumptions embedded in a statement that must be accepted as true for the sentence to make sense.
Example: “When did you stop procrastinating?”
(Assumes the person was procrastinating in the first place.)
Question: “What makes you think I was procrastinating?”
Complex Equivalence
Assuming two things mean the same, often without logical connection.
Example: “She didn’t call me back—she doesn’t care.”
Question: “How does not calling mean she doesn’t care?”
Disjunction
Using either/or language that implies limited choices, often creating a false dilemma.
Example: “Are you going to succeed or give up?”
Implied Causes
Statements that suggest a causal relationship without stating it directly.
Example: “If you cared about me, you’d be on time.”
(This implies caring causes punctuality.)
Tag Questions
Questions added to the end of a statement to encourage agreement or reduce resistance.
Example: “This is a good idea, isn’t it?”

sections.heading: Indirect language, stories and metaphor
sections.body:
Utilisation
The NLP technique of using whatever a person presents (emotions, objections, environment) as part of the intervention or communication.
Example: If someone says, “I’m nervous,” you might respond, “That nervous energy can help you stay alert and focused.”
Nesting
Embedding stories, ideas, or suggestions within one another to bypass resistance and engage the unconscious mind.
Example: A story within a story used to deliver a message or suggestion indirectly.
Extended Quotes
Attributing a message or suggestion to someone else to reduce resistance or make it more acceptable.
Example: “My mentor once told me, ‘You already have everything you need to succeed.’”
Spell Out Words
Using overly detailed or literal explanations of terms or phrases, often to clarify, confuse, or shift focus.
Example: Instead of saying “success,” you say, “S-U-C-C-E-S-S, that’s what you want, isn’t it?”
Conversational Postulate
A question that seems to ask for information but is actually a polite command or suggestion, often inviting action.
Example: “Can you open the window?”
(The expected response is action, not a yes/no answer.)
Selectional Restriction Violations
Using grammatically correct but semantically odd sentences that violate typical language patterns, often to provoke deeper thinking or a trance state.
Example: “The chair forgot the meeting.”
(Chairs can’t forget — this violation grabs attention.)
Metaphor
A figure of speech where one thing is described in terms of another to illustrate a point or influence subconsciously.
Example: “Life is a journey.”
Used in NLP to embed suggestions and reframe experience.

sections.heading: Responding to missing information and changing abstraction
sections.body:
Responding to Deletion
An NLP Meta-Model technique where missing information in someone’s language (e.g., “It’s hard”) is explored or questioned to uncover deeper meaning or clarify communication.
Persuasion by Chunking Up/Down
Influencing others by shifting the level of abstraction: chunking up to broader values or principles for alignment, or chunking down to specifics for clarity or proof.

title: Communication stances: the Satir categories in the notes

sections.heading: Five communication stances
sections.body:
The Blamer
One of Virginia Satir’s communication stances. This person deflects attention from themselves by criticizing others, often to feel more in control.
Example: “It’s your fault this went wrong!”
The Placater
Another Satir stance. This person avoids conflict by always agreeing, apologizing, or trying to please, often at the expense of their own needs.
Example: “It’s okay, I’ll do whatever you want. I just want you to be happy.”
The Computer
One of Virginia Satir’s communication stances. This person communicates with logic, facts, and calm detachment, often hiding emotions.
Example: “Statistically, this happens 40% of the time.”
They appear rational but disconnected.
Distracter
Another Satir stance. This person avoids the issue entirely by changing the subject or behaving unpredictably, often to avoid discomfort or confrontation.
Example: Responding to a serious question with a joke or random comment.
Leveler
The healthiest Satir stance. A person who communicates congruently—what they say, feel, and do are aligned.
Example: “I’m upset because this matters to me, and I’d like to talk about it calmly.”

sections.heading: The repeated communication model and congruence
sections.body:

A model developed by Virginia Satir that categorizes communication styles:
Placater: Seeks to please others, often at the expense of their own needs.
Blamer: Puts others down to avoid personal responsibility.
Super-Reasonable: Detached and logical, often avoiding emotions.
Irrelevant: Distracts or deflects attention to avoid issues.
Leveler: Communicates honestly and clearly, acknowledging emotions and facts.
Congruent / Incongruent
Congruent: A state where a person’s thoughts, feelings, and behaviors align and are consistent.
Incongruent: A mismatch between a person’s thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, often leading to confusion or discomfort.

sections.heading: Sensory language, evaluation and attention

Representational System Sort

Example:

Auditory: “That sounds right.”
Kinesthetic: “It feels good.”
Agree / Disagree
Describes whether a person tends to seek agreement or challenge what they hear.
Agree sorters look for common ground.
Disagree sorters tend to question or contradict by default.
Sensory / Intuitive
Refers to how a person gathers information:
Sensory types focus on facts, data, and direct experience.
Intuitive types look for patterns, impressions, and possibilities beyond what's directly observable.
Black & White / Continuum
Describes how people evaluate things:
Black & White thinkers see things as either/or, good/bad, right/wrong.
Continuum thinkers recognize shades of gray and prefer a spectrum or range.
Pessimist / Optimist
Focuses on whether a person tends to expect negative or positive outcomes:
Pessimists focus on what could go wrong.
Optimists focus on what could go right.
Certainty / Uncertainty
Refers to a person’s comfort with predictability:
Certainty sorters seek stability, clarity, and control.
Uncertainty sorters prefer novelty, variety, and flexibility.
Focus Sorting

Self-focus is inward (how it affects me).
Other-focus is outward (how it affects others).
Can also refer to task-focus vs. relationship-focus in certain contexts.

sections.heading: Purpose, problem orientation, change and reference frames
sections.body:
Why / How
Why people focus on purpose, reasons, and motivations.
“Why are we doing this?”
How people focus on procedures, steps, and methods.
“How do we do this?”
Origin / Solution
Origin-oriented individuals focus on the causes or history of a problem.
“How did this start?”
Solution-oriented individuals focus on resolving it.
“What can we do to fix it?”
Static / Process
Static thinkers view situations or people as fixed, unchanging.
“He is like that.”
Process thinkers see change, development, or evolution over time.
“He’s learning to be different.”
Analog / Digital
Analog thinking sees gradations and continuous variables—nuance.
“It’s somewhere between good and great.”
Digital thinking sees distinct, clear categories or yes/no states.
“It’s either good or bad.”
Emotional Coping
Refers to how a person deals with emotional experiences:
Constructive coping involves awareness and regulation.
Destructive coping might include avoidance, suppression, or projection.
(This is more psychological than strictly NLP, but relevant for profiling.)
Internal / External
Internal frame of reference means the person relies on their own standards and feelings.
“I know I did well.”
External frame of reference means the person looks to others for validation.
“Did I do okay? What did you think?”

sections.heading: Decision style, convincing, intensity and motivation
sections.body:
Feeling / Thinking
Feeling types prioritize emotions, values, and personal impact when processing or deciding.
Thinking types rely on logic, structure, and objective reasoning.
(This mirrors Jungian/MBTI preferences and is widely used in NLP.)
Active / Reflective / Inactive
Active: Prefers to take action quickly and learns by doing.
Reflective: Processes internally before acting, tends to analyze or consider options.
Inactive: Hesitant or disengaged—may struggle to commit to action or analysis.
Convincer
Describes how and when a person becomes convinced something is true or believable.
It includes:
Mode: What sensory channel convinces them (seeing, hearing, reading, doing).
Time: How often they need to experience something (once, several times, consistently, always).
Emotional Directional Sort
Toward: Motivated by goals, rewards, and desires.
“I want to achieve success.”
Away From: Motivated by avoiding problems or pain.
“I don’t want to fail.”
Intensity
Refers to how strongly someone experiences or expresses their emotional or sensory states.
High intensity: Feels deeply, reacts strongly.
Low intensity: More even-keeled or detached emotionally.
Towards / Away
Towards: Motivated by goals or positive outcomes.
Away: Motivated by avoiding problems or negative outcomes.
Past Assurance / Future Possibility
Past Assurance: Looks to past experiences for confidence.
Future Possibility: Focuses on future opportunities and what could happen.
Options / Procedure
Options: Prefers exploring multiple choices.
Procedure: Prefers following specific steps or routines.
Judging / Perceiving
Judging: Prefers structure and closure.
Perceiving: Prefers flexibility and spontaneity.

sections.heading: Values, responsibility, trust, social energy and the caution about labels
sections.body:
Necessity / Possibility / Impossibility / Desire
Necessity: Things that must be done.
Possibility: Things that could happen.
Impossibility: Things that cannot happen.
Desire: Things one wants to do.
Personal Interest
High: Strong personal involvement.
Low: Detached or impersonal.
Perfection / Optimization / Skepticism
Perfection: Strives for flawlessness and ideal outcomes.
Optimization: Focuses on improving or making something as effective as possible.
Skepticism: Doubts or questions information, seeking validation before accepting it.
Value Buying Sort
Refers to how a person makes decisions based on perceived value:
Value buyers prioritize long-term worth and benefits over immediate gratification.
Responsibility
Refers to how an individual takes ownership of tasks, outcomes, or decisions:
High responsibility: Takes ownership and accountability for actions.
Low responsibility: May defer or avoid taking responsibility.
Trust / Distrust
Trust: Believes in the reliability or honesty of others.
Distrust: Tends to doubt or question the reliability or intentions of others.
Introvert / Extrovert / Ambivert
Introvert: Prefers solitude and internal reflection.
Extrovert: Energized by social interaction and external stimuli.
Ambivert: Exhibits traits of both introversion and extroversion, depending on the situation.
Beware of All Labels
A caution against overgeneralizing or restricting understanding of people by rigid labels. Labels can limit or distort perception, as they don’t capture the full complexity of an individual.
Independent / Team Player / Manager
Independent: Prefers working alone and being self-reliant.
Team Player: Enjoys collaborating with others and working in groups.
Manager: Focuses on leading and organizing people, often balancing tasks and responsibilities.

sections.heading: Cooperation, social participation, information and motivation
sections.body:
Competitive / Cooperative / Polarity / Meta
Competitive: Focused on winning or outperforming others.
Cooperative: Prefers working with others towards a common goal.
Polarity: Refers to situations where there are two opposing viewpoints or forces (e.g., good vs. bad).
Meta: Refers to a higher-level view or abstraction of the situation or issue.
Socially: Active / Inactive / Both / Reflective
Active: Engages readily with others and enjoys socializing.
Inactive: Prefers solitude or less social interaction.
Both: Moves between social interaction and solitude depending on context.
Reflective: Prefers to think deeply and reflect internally rather than engaging actively in social situations.
Things / System / People / Information
Categories for organizing perspectives or focusing attention:
Things: Focus on objects, tasks, or tangible items.
System: Focus on processes, organization, or structures.
People: Focus on individuals or interpersonal dynamics.
Information: Focus on knowledge, facts, or data.
Quantitative / Qualitative
Quantitative: Focuses on measurable data, numbers, and statistical analysis.
Qualitative: Focuses on non-measurable aspects like experiences, feelings, and descriptions.
Knowledge Sort
Refers to how people categorize or prioritize information:
Knowledge sort involves organizing or sorting information based on relevance or importance to the individual, often aligning with their interests or goals.
Closure / Non-Closure
Closure: Preference for completing tasks or resolving situations quickly and definitively.
Non-Closure: Tolerates ambiguity or open-ended situations and may delay decision-making or closure.
Social Presentation
Refers to how individuals present themselves socially, either consciously or subconsciously. This can involve choosing how one expresses their identity, personality, and social roles in different contexts.
Power, Affiliation, and Achievement
These are key motivators according to McClelland’s Theory of Needs:
Power: Desire for influence and control over others.
Affiliation: Desire for relationships and social connections.
Achievement: Desire for success, mastery, and accomplishment.
Value Sort
Refers to how individuals prioritize their values, often involving a ranking system to determine what matters most to them (e.g., freedom, security, family, wealth).

sections.heading: Agency, confidence, time, processing and personal values
sections.body:
Strong-willed / Compliant / Stubborn
Strong-willed: Determined and resolute, willing to pursue their goals even in the face of obstacles.
Compliant: Willing to go along with others’ suggestions or authority.
Stubborn: Unyielding, often resistant to change, even when it’s not in their best interest.
Conditional / Unconditional
Conditional: Beliefs or actions dependent on certain conditions being met.
Unconditional: Beliefs or actions that are not dependent on any conditions or external factors.
Self Confidence: High / Low
High Self Confidence: Believes in their own abilities, decisions, and worth.
Low Self Confidence: Doubts their own abilities, often seeking validation or reassurance from others.
Mind / Emotion / Body / Role
Refers to the domains through which people interact with the world:
Mind: Cognitive processes, thoughts, and intellect.
Emotion: Feelings, moods, and emotional responses.
Body: Physical presence, sensations, and health.
Role: Social identity or positions in life (e.g., parent, leader, worker).
Self-integrity
Refers to maintaining personal values, consistency, and authenticity, acting in ways that align with one’s principles and beliefs.
Past / Present / Future
Refers to the time orientation of a person:
Past: Focuses on past experiences, memories, and history.
Present: Focuses on the here and now, living in the moment.
Future: Focuses on goals, plans, and what’s to come.
In-Time / Through-Time
In-Time: Focuses on the present moment, living in the "here and now." People who are "in-time" experience time as a continuous flow.
Through-Time: Focuses on a linear view of time, seeing the past, present, and future as distinct and moving "through" time. People who are "through-time" often reflect on the past and anticipate the future.
Concrete, Abstract, Random, and Sequential
These terms refer to how people organize and process information:
Concrete: Focus on specific, tangible details or facts.
Abstract: Focus on general concepts or ideas, often thinking in broad terms.
Random: Focus on patterns, connections, or spontaneity without a fixed structure.
Sequential: Focus on logical, step-by-step progression or order.
Ego / Strength
Ego: Refers to one’s sense of self, identity, and personal importance.
Strength: Refers to inner resilience, emotional fortitude, and personal power.
Morality
Refers to a person’s understanding of right and wrong, often influenced by cultural, social, or personal values. It relates to ethical principles guiding behavior and decision-making.

New Language Rapid Learning

Rhythmic Learning
Refers to a learning process that aligns with natural rhythms or cycles, such as incorporating patterns, repetition, and flow to facilitate understanding and retention.
The (Accelerated) Learning Chain
A concept in learning theory that describes the process of acquiring new information or skills through an accelerated, structured chain of steps. This method focuses on breaking down complex tasks into smaller, manageable pieces and reinforcing them quickly to speed up the learning process.
Apposition (of Opposite)
A technique used in communication or problem-solving, where two contrasting or opposite ideas are placed together to highlight the difference, often helping to clarify or resolve conflicts or tensions by understanding both sides.
Problem Definition
The process of clearly identifying and articulating the problem at hand. Effective problem definition includes understanding the underlying issues, constraints, and desired outcomes, providing clarity before attempting to find a solution.
Problem Solving Strategy
Refers to the approach or method used to address and resolve a problem. Common strategies include brainstorming, root cause analysis, trial and error, and using logic or creativity to identify solutions.
The D.V.P. Pattern
This stands for Deletions, Generalizations, and Distortions, which are key concepts in NLP (Neuro-Linguistic Programming). They describe how people filter, generalize, and distort information based on their perceptions. Understanding these patterns can help in clarifying communication and addressing misunderstandings.

Identifying Self-Sabotage Elements

The Binary Code of Forgetfulness

The Inner Peace Questionnaire
A tool or set of reflective questions designed to assess a person’s emotional balance, unresolved conflicts, and level of inner harmony.
Matrixing
The act of mapping out mental or emotional patterns—like a mental “matrix”—to identify connections between beliefs, behaviors, and outcomes for deeper insight or change.
Deconstructing Into Modalities
Breaking down an experience into its sensory components—visual, auditory, kinesthetic, etc.—to understand how it’s mentally represented and to allow for change or reprogramming.

title: The Art of War: Planning and assessment
summary: Compare purpose, conditions, leadership, discipline and preparation before committing resources.

sections.heading: Five factors in preparation
sections.body:
Art of War
Laying Plans
Sun Tzu said: The art of war is of vital importance to the State.
It is a matter of life and death, a road either to safety or to ruin. Hence it is a subject of inquiry which can on no account be neglected.
The art of war, then, is governed by five constant factors, to be taken into account in one’s deliberations, when seeking to determine the conditions obtaining in the field.
These are:
The Moral Law;
Heaven;
Earth;
The Commander;
Method and discipline.
The Moral Law causes the people to be in complete accord with their ruler, so that they will follow him regardless of their lives, undismayed by any danger.
Heaven signifies night and day, cold and heat, times and seasons.
Earth comprises distances, great and small; danger and security; open ground and narrow passes; the chances of life and death.
The Commander stands for the virtues of wisdom, sincerely, benevolence, courage and strictness.
By method and discipline are to be understood the marshalling of the army in its proper subdivisions, the graduations of rank among the officers, the maintenance of roads by which supplies may reach the army, and the control of military expenditure.
These five heads should be familiar to every general: he who knows them will be victorious; he who knows them not will fail.

sections.heading: Comparative assessment
sections.body:
Therefore, in your deliberations, when seeking to determine the military conditions, let them be made the basis of a comparison, in this wise:
Which of the two sovereigns is imbued with the Moral law?
Which of the two generals has the most ability?
With whom lie the advantages derived from Heaven and Earth?
On which side is discipline most rigorously enforced?
Which army is stronger?
On which side are officers and men more highly trained?
In which army is there the greater consistency both in reward and punishment?
By means of these seven considerations I can forecast victory or defeat.
The general that hearkens to my counsel and acts upon it, will conquer: let such a one be retained in command! The general that hearkens not to my counsel nor acts upon it, will suffer defeat:—let such a one be dismissed!
While heading the profit of my counsel, avail yourself also of any helpful circumstances over and beyond the ordinary rules.
As circumstances are favourable, one should modify one’s plans.

sections.heading: Deception and preparation in the historical text
sections.body:
All warfare is based on deception.
Hence, when able to attack, we must seem unable; when using our forces, we must seem inactive; when we are near, we must make the enemy believe we are far away; when far away, we must make him believe we are near.
Hold out baits to entice the enemy. Feign disorder, and crush him.
If he is secure at all points, be prepared for him. If he is in superior strength, evade him.
If he is taking his ease, give him no rest. If his forces are united, separate them.
If your opponent is of choleric temper, seek to irritate him. Pretend to be weak, that he may grow arrogant.
Attack him where he is unprepared, appear where you are not expected.
These military devices, leading to victory, must not be divulged beforehand.
Now the general who wins a battle makes many calculations in his temple where the battle is fought. The general who loses a battle makes a few calculations beforehand. Thus doing many calculations lead to victory, and few calculations to defeat: how much more no calculation at all! It is by attention to this point that I can foresee who is likely to win or lose.

title: The Art of War: Campaign costs and duration
